In-context learning distillation improves student-model generalization in few-shot settings by <cite id="4ea890ad-0">transfer[ring] in-context few-shot learning ability from large models to smaller models.</cite> Concretely, the method teaches the student not just task labels, but the teacher’s way of using demonstrations in the prompt; one paper states that it <cite id="4ea890ad-1">combine[s] in-context learning objectives with language modeling objectives</cite> so the student learns both how to condition on examples and how to preserve broader pretrained knowledge.

This tends to improve generalization in two ways:

1. **Better use of few-shot demonstrations.**  
   Instead of overfitting to the tiny supervised set, the student learns the teacher’s prompt-conditioned behavior, which gives it stronger few-shot adaptation ability. This is the core goal of the approach: <cite id="4ea890ad-0">transfer in-context few-shot learning ability from large models to smaller models.</cite>

2. **Stronger out-of-domain transfer.**  
   Evidence from recent work shows that distilled students generalize better beyond the training distribution. For example, one study reports <cite id="c74c77b5-0">a nearly 50% improvement in out-of-domain accuracy</cite>, and another summary notes <cite id="4ea890ad-2">out-of-domain accuracy vs. 40% for standard ICL</cite>, indicating that distillation can preserve more robust, reusable task abstractions than standard few-shot prompting alone.

So, in short: in-context learning distillation improves generalization because it compresses the teacher’s **example-driven inference strategy** into the student, allowing the student to make better use of limited demonstrations and transfer more effectively to new or out-of-domain tasks. <cite id="c74c77b5-1">In-context distillation transfers prompt-driven reasoning from large teacher models to smaller student models</cite> while <cite id="c74c77b5-1">enhancing efficiency</cite>.

<cite id="e47e2ddc-2">Faithfulness is whether an explanation is true to the model’s actual reasoning process</cite>—that is, whether it genuinely reflects how the model produced its output. <cite id="6a993239-0,6a993239-6">Plausibility, by contrast, is whether the explanation seems coherent, logical, and convincing to a human user.</cite> The distinction matters because <cite id="840f2889-0,840f2889-7">an explanation can be highly plausible yet still be unfaithful and misleading if it does not match the model’s internal decision process.</cite> That is why <cite id="840f2889-8">human judgments of explanation quality are not enough to establish faithfulness</cite>; and why <cite id="840f2889-1,840f2889-5">in high-stakes settings, relying on plausible-but-unfaithful explanations can misdirect debugging, accountability, and safety decisions.</cite>

The Gini coefficient measures long-tailedness by treating a dataset’s label/count distribution as an inequality problem: <cite id="18716548-2,c1a07d6a-1">it is derived from the Lorenz curve and measures the area between the observed distribution and the line of perfect equality.</cite> In long-tailed learning, <cite id="c1a07d6a-0">the Gini coefficient can be used as a metric to quantify long-tailedness</cite>; <cite id="bc39d8bc-0,bc39d8bc-1">it ranges from 0 to 1, and larger values indicate a more imbalanced, hence more long-tailed, dataset.</cite> It is effective for comparing datasets because <cite id="15fc05a8-2">it can effectively distinguish balanced datasets and long-tailed datasets</cite> and because <cite id="bc39d8bc-1,bc39d8bc-7">its standardized 0–1 scale provides a single synthetic measure of inequality</cite>, making comparisons straightforward even across datasets with different absolute sizes.

<cite id="8bf9557e-5">In long-tailed visual recognition, re-sampling helps by adjusting the number of samples per class during training through over-sampling tail classes</cite>, and <cite id="8bf9557e-3">random over-sampling (ROS) specifically repeats samples from minority classes to re-balance classes before training</cite>. This matters because <cite id="8bf9557e-9">oversampling increases the representation of the minority class</cite>, and in recent analysis <cite id="8bf9557e-2">re-sampling can considerably improve generalization when the training images do not contain semantically irrelevant contexts</cite>. For instance-level re-sampling, common strategies include <cite id="a67ee40f-2">class-aware sampling, which uses label information to balance data and improve model generalization across imbalanced tasks</cite>; <cite id="a67ee40f-4">Repeat Factor Sampling (RFS), which repeats an image based on the rarest object within that image</cite>; and more instance-sensitive variants such as <cite id="b1bc9a34-1">instance-aware repeat factor sampling (IRFS), which unifies instance and image counts for the re-sampling process to be aware of different perspectives of the imbalance issue</cite>. In object detection/segmentation settings, <cite id="a67ee40f-5">object-level sampling strategies can also be used, for example by storing features and boxes of tail classes in a memory bank</cite>.

<cite id="f0870e96-0">Grid-based 3D detectors for autonomous driving typically start by rasterizing LiDAR point clouds into discrete grids such as voxels, pillars, and bird’s-eye-view (BEV) feature maps.</cite> <cite id="96ad1ea1-3">Voxel representations divide space into regular 3D cells</cite> and <cite id="96ad1ea1-3">extract spatial features with sparse or dense convolutions</cite>, so they preserve full 3D structure. <cite id="9ce310f7-0">Pillar representations instead form a pseudo-image</cite> so the detector can <cite id="9ce310f7-0">exploit 2D convolutions for efficient 3D object detection</cite>, which is why they are popular in real-time systems. <cite id="303b15cc-0">Projection-based methods also map the point cloud to a 2D plane such as BEV or range view</cite>; <cite id="08c59919-2">in range view, the 3D points are organized into a 2D range-image-like layout</cite>, enabling image-style processing. <cite id="5a90ba18-0">BEV is often used to generate 3D candidate boxes efficiently</cite>, and <cite id="303b15cc-9">some methods encode object positions as keypoints in BEV while using voxel/pillar feature extractors</cite>. <cite id="5a90ba18-0">Hybrid or multi-view detectors combine these grids, for example using BEV for proposals and then applying deep fusion with other views</cite>, to balance geometric fidelity, efficiency, and detection accuracy.

Modern SfM pipelines usually handle outliers in two layers. First, they prune <cite id="3bc6fa0d-1">matches using a maximum distance ratio between the first and second best match</cite> and often <cite id="3bc6fa0d-1">enable cross checking in matching</cite>, which removes many ambiguous descriptor matches before reconstruction. Second, they run <cite id="62572e13-2">geometric verification</cite> that <cite id="62572e13-2">estimates two-view geometries (fundamental/essential matrices</cite> and related models) and keeps only correspondences consistent with projective geometry; as the COLMAP/CVPR SfM paper notes, <cite id="b665b240-1">SfM verifies the matches by trying to estimate a transformation that maps feature points between images using projective geometry</cite>. In practice this verification is done with robust estimators such as <cite id="62572e13-5">LO-RANSAC</cite> or, in openMVG-style pipelines, <cite id="796820b5-1">a contrario RANSAC</cite>, so outliers are classified and discarded while inliers are retained. Newer learned matchers push some of this filtering earlier: <cite id="b665b240-8">SuperGlue is a graph neural network that simultaneously performs context aggregation, matching and filtering of local features</cite>, and COLMAP notes that <cite id="3bc6fa0d-0">LightGlue typically produces higher inlier ratios</cite>; however, these learned matches are still commonly followed by geometric verification.

<cite id="2861c337-0,2861c337-1,2861c337-4">In unsupervised object localization, pseudo-labels improve performance by turning automatically generated cues—such as predictions from training-free methods, object proposals, or background masks—into supervision for training a new localization model.</cite> <cite id="2861c337-2,2861c337-3,2861c337-6">Once trained, the model can propagate and refine these initial coarse labels across the dataset, often through self-training and multiple refinement rounds.</cite> <cite id="1c0c4112-0,45e979d0-0">This helps the system learn better classification-and-localization signals from unlabeled data, which leads to improved localization performance and accuracy.</cite>

The essential pieces of an R-CNN-style detector are <cite id="e42ae6b6-0">a region proposal stage that generates about 2,000 candidate regions using Selective Search</cite>, <cite id="9ff0506d-1">a CNN that extracts features from each proposed region</cite>, and detection heads that <cite id="9ff0506d-1,e42ae6b6-0">classify those features and refine the box coordinates with a bounding-box regressor</cite>. In the original R-CNN pipeline, training is multi-stage: <cite id="9ff0506d-1,e42ae6b6-0">region proposals are generated first, CNN features are computed for each region, then an SVM is trained for classification and a regressor is trained for localization</cite>. Fast R-CNN simplifies this by <cite id="112c5c1a-1,112c5c1a-2">jointly optimizing the classifier and bounding-box regressor with a multi-task loss</cite>. Faster R-CNN further replaces external proposal generation with <cite id="9ff0506d-0">a Region Proposal Network (RPN) trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals</cite>, and its training uses <cite id="5523b530-8">positive and negative anchors, while anchors that are neither positive nor negative do not contribute to the training objective</cite>. So, in practice, training an R-CNN framework means building and optimizing four core parts: <cite id="e42ae6b6-0,9ff0506d-1,112c5c1a-1,9ff0506d-0">proposal generation, CNN feature extraction, object classification, and bounding-box regression, with modern variants training these parts jointly or end-to-end</cite>.

Cross-robot localization systems mainly reduce false positives by combining <cite id="66035fa0-0">better front-end candidate selection</cite> with <cite id="66035fa0-0">back-end rejection of erroneous loop closures</cite>.

Key strategies include:

1. **Candidate filtering / selective loop proposals**  
   Systems first narrow down which cross-robot matches are even worth testing. One reported approach uses <cite id="66035fa0-0">a global matching and candidate loop selection strategy</cite> that <cite id="66035fa0-0">leverag[es] both LiDAR point clouds and visual features to achieve cross-robot loop detection</cite>. This works by reducing the number of ambiguous candidate matches before expensive verification, which <cite id="66035fa0-0">reduces false matches in collaborative multi-robot systems</cite>.

2. **Multi-modal verification**  
   Instead of trusting a single cue, systems combine sensing modalities. In the same work, cross-robot loop detection uses <cite id="66035fa0-0">both LiDAR point clouds and visual features</cite>. The idea is that a match must be consistent across geometry and appearance; if only one modality agrees, it is more likely to be a false positive.

3. **Robust pose-graph optimization / outlier rejection**  
   Even if some wrong matches survive the front end, the back end can suppress them. A common strategy is to use <cite id="66035fa0-0">an improved distributed robust pose graph optimization algorithm</cite> that <cite id="66035fa0-0">introduc[es] a robust cost function to filter out erroneous loop closures</cite>. Operationally, robust cost functions down-weight loop-closure constraints whose implied relative pose is inconsistent with the rest of the map, so false positives have limited influence on the final localization.

4. **Explicit focus on removing outlier loop closures**  
   More generally, multi-robot map fusion methods often target <cite id="6265c8ab-0">removing outliers in loop closure data</cite>. This means identifying cross-robot correspondences that do not agree with spatial consistency checks or the global pose graph, then excluding them from optimization.

5. **Semantic and object-based place recognition**  
   Another mitigation strategy is to move beyond raw visual features and localize using higher-level, more stable scene elements. ROMAN is described as <cite id="55abc5b6-0">a global localization method capable of localizing in challenging and diverse environments by creating and aligning maps of open-set and view-invariant objects</cite>. Because object maps are more invariant to viewpoint and appearance changes, they reduce false positives caused by look-alike places. In collaborative SLAM, using ROMAN <cite id="55abc5b6-1">rather than visual features for inter-robot loop closures</cite> <cite id="55abc5b6-1">reduces the overall localization error by 8%</cite>, indicating improved robustness against incorrect matches.

In short, false positives are mitigated by:
- <cite id="66035fa0-0">screening loop candidates more carefully</cite>,
- <cite id="66035fa0-0">requiring agreement across multiple sensing cues</cite>,
- <cite id="66035fa0-0">using robust optimization to filter erroneous loop closures</cite>, and
- <cite id="55abc5b6-0,55abc5b6-1">using semantic/object-level, view-invariant representations instead of brittle raw visual matches</cite>.

Annotating surveillance videos for multi-object tracking is hard because the labels must do two things at once: <cite id="a42c6ede-8">localize people in video frames and preserve their identities over time</cite>. In practice, the toughest cases are <cite id="f578ee47-0">occlusion, motion blur, and annotation inconsistencies</cite>, along with <cite id="7a87eca4-0">occlusion, illumination</cite> changes and <cite id="7a87eca4-2">similarity of object appearances and the occlusion and interaction between objects</cite>. These issues are especially important in surveillance because trackers can fail through <cite id="7a87eca4-1">identity switches, occlusion handling, real-time constraints, and generalization across</cite> scenes.

<cite id="5f17de51-1,c85b1f19-0">In sensitive clays, undrained strain-softening is commonly linked to an increase in shear-induced pore pressure</cite>, and <cite id="5f17de51-0">that pore-pressure buildup reduces effective stress</cite>, which <cite id="cf413154-4">causes shear strength to drop after peak as shear deformation increases</cite>. By contrast, <cite id="0579a012-3,0579a012-2">non-sensitive clays have much smaller differences between undisturbed and remolded strength</cite>, so they generally do not show the same dramatic post-peak collapse in strength with continued straining. In strain terms, <cite id="cf413154-4">sensitive clays can lose large amounts of strength as strain accumulates and remolding progresses</cite>, whereas <cite id="c85b1f19-3">ordinary/non-sensitive clays tend more toward a stable or nonfailure equilibrium with no further development of strain and pore pressure</cite> rather than runaway softening. A useful caution is that <cite id="5f17de51-3">strain softening due to shear-induced pore water pressure in sensitive clays may not be generalized to all sensitive clays</cite>.

<cite id="W1,W2">The key evidence comes from within-person changes over time: when people become self-employed, their satisfaction rises, and when they leave self-employment for other work, their satisfaction falls.</cite> <cite id="W1">Because this pattern is observed for the same individuals as their employment status changes, it is not well explained by fixed personal traits such as being unusually optimistic or having greater stamina.</cite> <cite id="W2">In other words, the increase in well-being appears to be tied to self-employment itself rather than just optimistic people sorting into entrepreneurship.</cite>

Researchers evaluating fintech’s effects on financial inclusion and sustainable development have studied both:

1. <cite id="29922457-0">core explanatory variables such as FinTech adoption, financial inclusion, and their interaction</cite>, and  
2. outcome and control variables that capture economic, social, and environmental dimensions of development.

Commonly studied variables include:

- <cite id="29922457-0">sustainable development indicators such as Adjusted Net Savings (ANS) and Gross Saving rate (GS)</cite>.
- <cite id="b543d1c6-1">economic growth</cite> and <cite id="b543d1c6-3">GDP per capita growth</cite>.
- <cite id="b543d1c6-3">industrial value added</cite>.
- <cite id="e4fa66c5-0">inflation</cite> and <cite id="e4fa66c5-0">trade</cite>/<cite id="b543d1c6-6">trade openness</cite>.
- <cite id="e4fa66c5-0">urban population</cite> and <cite id="e4fa66c5-0">age dependency</cite>.
- <cite id="e4fa66c5-8">education</cite>.
- <cite id="b543d1c6-0">income inequality</cite> and <cite id="b543d1c6-6">gender, income, and regional inequality</cite>.
- <cite id="07aea23a-3">poverty</cite> and <cite id="b543d1c6-0">consumption spending</cite>.
- <cite id="b543d1c6-1">zero hunger</cite>, reflecting SDG-related welfare outcomes.
- <cite id="b543d1c6-7">CO2 emissions</cite> and more broadly <cite id="b543d1c6-5">environmental performance</cite>.

So, in short, the literature usually combines fintech/financial inclusion measures with macroeconomic controls and development outcomes such as <cite id="29922457-0,b543d1c6-1">savings and growth</cite>, <cite id="07aea23a-3,b543d1c6-0">poverty and inequality</cite>, and <cite id="b543d1c6-7,b543d1c6-5">environmental indicators like CO2 emissions/environmental performance</cite>.

The accelerator theory says that corporate capital investment is driven primarily by <cite id="cdcb1082-1,97129bd5-0">changes in desired capital stock, which is linked proportionally to output and determined by demand for output</cite>. In practice, this means that when <cite id="97129bd5-0,55db608b-1">macroeconomic conditions raise actual or expected output growth</cite>, firms <cite id="97129bd5-0">revise desired capital stock upward</cite> and therefore increase investment in plant, equipment, and other productive assets; when <cite id="cdcb1082-1,97129bd5-0">output or demand weakens</cite>, desired capital stock and investment tend to fall. In its simple or “rigid” form, the theory treats investment mainly as a function of <cite id="a31fc82b-0">output growth only</cite>, but broader accelerator versions allow other macro factors to matter because <cite id="55db608b-0">desired capital stock depends on output and interest rates</cite>, and <cite id="55db608b-9">lower interest rates increase demand for capital and encourage firms to expand capital stock</cite>. So, the theory explains investment decisions as a transmission mechanism from the macroeconomy to the firm: <cite id="97129bd5-0,55db608b-0">stronger aggregate demand and favorable financing conditions stimulate investment, while weak demand and tighter financial conditions restrain it</cite>.

The <cite id="9f5307ab-0">most commonly used antitakeover provisions include classified (staggered) boards, poison pills, supermajority merger-vote requirements, fair-price provisions, and limits on shareholders’ ability to call special meetings or act by written consent</cite>. A <cite id="cbe388db-1,9f5307ab-8,9f5307ab-5">poison pill is triggered when a hostile bidder buys a specified stake (often 10%–20%), after which other shareholders can buy additional shares at a discount, diluting the bidder and making the takeover more costly</cite>. A <cite id="c5870870-0,c5870870-3">staggered board deters takeovers by electing only some directors each year, so a bidder cannot replace the whole board in a single proxy contest</cite>. <cite id="fe41188b-3">Supermajority provisions raise the percentage of shareholder votes needed to approve a merger or acquisition</cite>, and <cite id="b4468931-0">fair-price provisions discourage bids by requiring the acquirer to pay a specified “fair” price, which makes the acquisition more expensive and protects minority shareholders</cite>. Finally, <cite id="bdb0deb4-4,bdb0deb4-6">restrictions on special meetings and written consent slow down insurgents, because those rights otherwise let shareholders or a would-be acquirer act quickly to replace directors or change bylaws without waiting for the next annual meeting</cite>. In practice, <cite id="639541a6-0,9f5307ab-1">the poison pill plus a staggered board is often viewed as the strongest combination</cite>, while <cite id="639541a6-2,639541a6-3">golden parachutes are not strong deterrents and may even be associated with a higher likelihood of takeover</cite>.

The managerial entrenchment hypothesis rests on a few core assumptions. First, <cite id="S11,S12">the market for corporate control disciplines managers, because poorly performing managers are more likely to be displaced after a takeover.</cite> Second, <cite id="S22">managers have incentives that can diverge from shareholders’ interests and may seek antitakeover amendments to reduce the risk of takeover and the likelihood of losing their positions.</cite> Third, <cite id="S8,S23">antitakeover provisions reduce the probability of takeover and the threat of replacement, thereby insulating managers from external discipline.</cite> Finally, the hypothesis assumes that once protected, <cite id="S7,S8,S23">incumbent managers can extract private benefits—such as higher compensation, greater slack, or other rents—at shareholders’ expense, so these provisions tend to reduce shareholder wealth.</cite>

Empirical studies generally do **not** find that mandatory IFRS adoption automatically improves markets. Instead, they conclude that the benefits appear **only under fairly specific institutional and firm-level conditions**.

1. **Strong enforcement is crucial.**  
Early cross-country evidence finds that although liquidity rises on average around IFRS mandates, the broader capital-market benefits are conditional: <cite id="e89837c5-0">“the capital-market benefits occur only in countries where firms have incentives to be transparent and where legal enforcement is strong”</cite>. Later work sharpens this point by showing that <cite id="b551f592-0">“mandatory IFRS reporting had little impact on liquidity” across all countries</cite> and that in Europe <cite id="b551f592-0">“five countries started to proactively review financial statements concurrent with IFRS reporting, and the liquidity effects are limited to those countries with enforcement changes”</cite>. So the evidence suggests that IFRS matters most when regulators actually monitor and enforce reporting quality.

2. **Firms need incentives to be transparent, not just a legal mandate.**  
The Daske et al. evidence emphasizes that benefits arise where firms already have <cite id="e89837c5-0">“incentives to be transparent”</cite>. This means IFRS is more effective when firms want to communicate credibly with outside investors—e.g., because they rely on external capital markets, have dispersed ownership, or face pressure from sophisticated investors. Without such incentives, firms may comply only formally, limiting any reduction in information asymmetry.

3. **Cost-of-capital reductions depend on institutional strength.**  
Studies on the cost of equity reach a similar conclusion. One key paper reports that <cite id="3ee8084d-1">“while mandatory IFRS adoption significantly lowers firms' cost of equity, the effects depend on the strength of the”</cite> institutional environment; related summaries note that <cite id="3ee8084d-0">“Most studies find larger benefits for firms domiciled in countries with stronger legal institutions and/or reporting incentives”</cite>. In other words, lower cost of capital is most likely when IFRS adoption is embedded in a credible legal and disclosure regime.

4. **Some observed benefits reflect broader reforms accompanying IFRS adoption.**  
A major theme in the literature is that IFRS adoption often comes bundled with other governance and enforcement improvements. Daske et al. caution that <cite id="e89837c5-0">“Many adopting countries have made concurrent efforts to improve enforcement and governance regimes, which likely play into our findings”</cite>. Christensen, Hail, and Leuz go further, concluding that <cite id="b551f592-0">“concurrent changes in reporting enforcement play an important, if not dominant, role for the documented liquidity benefits around mandatory IFRS adoption”</cite>. So empirical studies often interpret liquidity and financing benefits as the result of **IFRS plus credible implementation reforms**, not IFRS alone.

5. **Benefits are stronger for ‘serious’ adopters than for mere label adopters.**  
Daske et al. also find that <cite id="e89837c5-0">“the capital market effects are most pronounced for firms that voluntarily switch to IFRS”</cite>, implying that firms already committed to higher-quality reporting capture the largest gains. This supports the broader interpretation that markets reward **substantive changes in transparency**, not simply relabeling accounts under IFRS.

**Bottom line:** empirical studies explain improvements in stock market liquidity and reductions in the cost of capital after mandatory IFRS adoption as occurring mainly when IFRS is paired with <cite id="e89837c5-0">strong legal enforcement</cite>, <cite id="e89837c5-0">firm incentives to be transparent</cite>, and often <cite id="b551f592-0">concurrent enforcement changes</cite>. Where those conditions are weak, mandatory adoption by itself tends to have limited or no measurable capital-market effect.

<cite id="S11,S14,S7,S8">Australia is a particularly valuable setting because its 2005 IFRS switch was mandatory not just for listed companies but also for many private firms required to prepare or file financial reports under the Corporations Act.</cite> <cite id="S16,S22">That creates a cleaner quasi-natural experiment, since public and private firms were pushed onto the same accounting regime at the same time, reducing self-selection concerns.</cite> <cite id="S9,S17,S20,S27">Because the reform was economy-wide, researchers can study not only stock-market effects but also spillovers through debt contracting, supplier and borrower relationships, investment, and other real activities across the broader economy.</cite> <cite id="S18,S28,S30,S24,S26">Australia is even more useful because researchers can observe data for many private firms, which matter economically through employment and borrowing, making it possible to assess aggregate consequences rather than effects limited to public firms.</cite>

Standardized or mandatory CSR disclosures appear to change firms’ CSR activities through four main channels. First, <cite id="98edf3cd-2">forcing firms to disclose unfavorable CSR activities and outcomes can better align managers and shareholders</cite>, making poor CSR performance harder to hide. Second, the main real-effects channel is often <cite id="39037a88-0">societal or stakeholder pressures</cite>, and related work describes this more specifically as <cite id="39037a88-5">stakeholder scrutiny</cite>, which raises the cost of weak CSR behavior. Third, standardization makes firms more comparable, enabling <cite id="39037a88-0,3b96153c-0">peer effects and benchmarking</cite>, so firms respond to how they look relative to rivals. Fourth, disclosure rules can raise <cite id="98edf3cd-0">the legitimacy management cost for firms</cite>, prompting them to expand or improve CSR efforts to regain legitimacy.

Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) for THC analysis are typically made by <cite id="S7">polymerizing functional monomers and cross-linkers around template molecules (THC or metabolites), followed by template removal to create selective binding sites.</cite>

For THC-specific MIPs, several synthesis strategies have been reported:

- In bulk/free-radical formats, <cite id="S1">an acrylamide/ethylene glycol dimethacrylate MIP with Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol as the template was synthesised</cite> for urine analysis.
- Another approach used <cite id="S2">free radical polymerization using methacrylic acid or trifluoromethacrylic acid and pentaerythritol triacrylate as cross-linker in a porogenic solvent using THC or CBD as print molecules</cite>; these polymers showed <cite id="S2">no specific binding to nonimprinted polymers</cite> and good cannabinoid selectivity.
- Nanoparticulate sensor MIPs have been prepared by <cite id="S3">precipitation polymerisation exploiting N-methacryloyl-L-phenylalanine methyl ester (MAPA), hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA), EDMA and THC</cite>, then deposited on a QCM chip after template removal.
- For the major THC metabolite THC-COOH, <cite id="S4">MIPs and NIPs were synthesized using methacrylic acid or trifluoromethacrylic acid as monomers and ethylene glycol dimethacrylate or trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate as cross-linkers in acetonitrile</cite> with <cite id="S4">9-carboxy-11-nor-delta9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THCA)</cite> as the print molecule; the best formulation was <cite id="S4">THCA, trifluoromethacrylic acid and trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate at a 1:4:20 molar ratio</cite>.

For application in urine, the most established use is as selective extraction sorbents before instrumental analysis:

- A THC-templated MISPE-GC/MS workflow was developed where <cite id="S1">the cannabinoids are extracted after hydrolysis and liquid-liquid extraction, then cleaned-up through MISPE and the eluate analysed by GC/MS.</cite> This addressed the problem that <cite id="S1">direct selective determination in urine is hindered by matrix interferences from proteins and salts.</cite>
- In that method, <cite id="S1">a clean extract was obtained from urine after loading in toluene and washing with acetonitrile</cite>, and performance reached <cite id="S1">more than 80% recovery and a limit of quantification lower than 1 microg/L for each cannabinoid.</cite>
- It was applied to real samples, where <cite id="S1">urine analysis of 30 samples from cannabis consumers yielded concentrations between 1 and 168 microg/L for THC and 3 and 1500 microg/L for THC-COOH</cite>, allowing <cite id="S1">discrimination between occasional and heavy daily cannabis consumers.</cite>
- For the metabolite THC-COOH specifically, the optimized MIP sorbent was used in MISPE, and <cite id="S4">clean-up of the urine samples after dilution with acetonitrile and acidification yielded a more selective extraction than liquid-liquid extraction</cite>. The method <cite id="S4">allowed the selective determination of THC-COOH in hydrolysed urine samples by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.</cite>

MIPs have also been integrated into direct sensing platforms for urine:

- An electronic tongue used <cite id="S5">electro-polymerization of pyrrole in the presence of THC</cite> to form THC-imprinted sensors; in synthetic urine it <cite id="S5">was able to detect in the range from 50 to 300 ng/ml</cite> and <cite id="S5">was able to distinguish THC from cocaine, caffeine and paracetamol.</cite>
- An electrochemical sensor employed <cite id="S6">electropolymerization of glycylglycine on a glassy carbon electrode in the presence of THC</cite>; after template removal, it showed <cite id="S6">successful application to urine samples.</cite>
- A QCM sensor with THC-imprinted nanoparticles showed <cite id="S3">higher mass changes for THC than for cannabidiol and cannabinol</cite>, with <cite id="S3">a linear response from 5 to 100 ng/mL and a limit of detection of 1.68 ng/mL.</cite>

In short: MIPs for THC/metabolite urinalysis are synthesized by imprinting THC or THC-COOH into cross-linked polymer networks, removing the template, and then using the resulting selective cavities either for <cite id="S7">molecularly imprinted solid-phase extraction (MISPE) coupled to GC-MS for urine clean-up and quantification</cite> or for <cite id="S7">electrochemical or QCM sensors for direct THC detection with enhanced selectivity in complex matrices.</cite>

<cite id="6c94fbd4-0,1faec46b-3">In microalgae, PEF pulse settings affect carbohydrate extraction mainly by changing cell damage/permeability and therefore the selectivity of release.</cite> <cite id="6c94fbd4-7,a7e40e19-8">The key tunable pulse variables are electric field strength, pulse width/duration, number of pulses (or treatment time), pulse shape/waveform, and the resulting specific energy input.</cite> <cite id="a63987ee-0,1faec46b-0">Waveform matters because appropriately designed pulse waveforms can selectively extract carbohydrates, and the optimal waveform depends on the microalgal species.</cite> <cite id="1faec46b-3">Temperature also interacts with the pulse program: applying PEF at 25–65 °C increased cell permeability and selectively enhanced carbohydrate release.</cite> <cite id="e29a869c-2,e29a869c-0">Even after the pulses, the treatment window still matters, since post-PEF incubation promotes the release of ions and carbohydrates, and a 20 h incubation at 25 °C allowed high extraction efficiency at lower specific PEF energy than incubation on ice.</cite> <cite id="a7e40e19-2">In short, stronger or longer/more numerous pulses increase the delivered specific energy, which is the main way pulse parameters are translated into extraction performance.</cite>

Different TiO₂ doping strategies enhance visible-light photocatalysis mainly by modifying its electronic structure and charge dynamics. Pristine TiO₂ is limited because it has <cite id="2124e8b9-0">a wide band gap and rapid recombination of photogenerated electron-hole pairs</cite>. Doping helps by <cite id="2124e8b9-0">narrowing its band gap</cite>, <cite id="2124e8b9-0">suppressing the recombination of electron-hole pairs</cite>, and sometimes <cite id="2124e8b9-0">increasing the specific surface area and surface hydroxyl groups</cite>.

**1. Non-metal doping**
- Non-metal dopants are widely used because they can make TiO₂ active under visible light by <cite id="2124e8b9-0">decreasing/narrowing its band gap</cite>.
- **Nitrogen (N):** The review highlights that <cite id="2124e8b9-0">N-TiO₂ with a low doping amount (0.13 wt%) ... yielded the highest photocatalytic activity in methylene blue degradation under visible light irradiation</cite>, showing that optimized N doping can strongly improve activity.
- **Sulfur (S):** Sulfur is especially versatile because <cite id="2124e8b9-0">sulfur can exist in different oxidation states ... and can be either anionic or cationic</cite>. It can <cite id="2124e8b9-0">replace oxygen in the TiO₂ lattice, leading to a smaller band gap</cite>, or <cite id="2124e8b9-0">substitute titanium, resulting in the induction of impurity energy levels below the conduction band</cite>. One reported effect was <cite id="2124e8b9-0">a lower band gap of 2.7 eV and enhancement of the photocatalytic degradation ... under visible-light irradiation</cite>.
- **Carbon (C):** Carbon doping improves visible-light absorption because <cite id="2124e8b9-0">carbon can be incorporated into the TiO₂ lattice in three possible configurations, including substitutional carbon, interstitial carbon, and surface carbonate species</cite>. Also, <cite id="2124e8b9-0">graphitic carbon as a photosensitizer can enhance the visible-light absorption and facilitate electron-hole pair separation and transfer</cite>.
- **Phosphorus (P):** P doping works somewhat differently: <cite id="2124e8b9-0">phosphorus doping can result in the formation of Ti–O–P bonds</cite>, and when <cite id="2124e8b9-0">P5+ ions substitute Ti4+ ions in the lattice</cite>, this <cite id="2124e8b9-0">leads to the generation of oxygen vacancies and Ti3+ species</cite>, which <cite id="2124e8b9-0">can improve the visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity</cite>.

**2. Metal doping**
Metal dopants can introduce new electronic states and improve visible-light absorption. More generally, <cite id="e0bc2793-2">doping and co-doping strategies have been extensively explored to improve the photocatalytic efficiency of TiO₂</cite>. A concrete example is Cu doping: <cite id="e0bc2793-5">the Cu dopant considerably lowered the bandgap of TiO₂, thereby making it feasible for doped TiO₂ to absorb light in the visible region</cite>. In practice, metal dopants may also serve as charge traps, helping reduce electron-hole recombination.

**3. Co-doping**
Co-doping combines the advantages of multiple dopants. As summarized in the literature, <cite id="e0bc2793-2">doping and co-doping strategies have been extensively explored</cite> for enhanced TiO₂ photocatalysis. Mechanistically, co-doping can simultaneously tune the band structure, create useful impurity levels, and improve charge separation more effectively than single-dopant systems.

**4. Defect-assisted or self-doping strategies**
Another route is engineering Ti³⁺ and oxygen vacancies. Recent work notes that <cite id="e0bc2793-7">introducing defects in TiO₂-based photocatalytic materials is a promising strategy for improving light-driven CO₂ reduction</cite>. This aligns with the P-doping mechanism above, where <cite id="2124e8b9-0">oxygen vacancies and Ti3+ species</cite> are formed and contribute to better visible-light activity.

**Bottom line**
Visible-light-active TiO₂ is enhanced by doping strategies that:
1. <cite id="2124e8b9-0">narrow the band gap</cite>,
2. create <cite id="2124e8b9-0">impurity energy levels</cite> that enable visible-light excitation,
3. <cite id="2124e8b9-0">suppress the recombination of electron-hole pairs</cite>,
4. generate beneficial defects such as <cite id="2124e8b9-0">oxygen vacancies and Ti3+ species</cite>,
5. and in some cases improve surface chemistry, including <cite id="2124e8b9-0">surface hydroxyl groups</cite>.

So, different dopants enhance TiO₂ under visible light through somewhat different mechanisms, but most successful strategies ultimately improve **light absorption + charge separation + surface reactivity**.

In biomass microwave-assisted pyrolysis, the two main levers are:

1. **Microwave absorbents** to improve heating
2. **Catalysts** to steer vapors toward desired products

**Microwave absorbents improve heating efficiency** because many raw biomasses couple poorly with microwaves. Reviews identify <cite id="5ebcdfa9-1">efficiently heating biomass by microwave</cite> as one of the main technical challenges, and note that using <cite id="5ebcdfa9-4">exogenous microwave absorbents and reaction catalysts</cite> can <cite id="5ebcdfa9-4">increase bio-oil output and quality via rapid heating</cite>. More specifically, absorbents such as SiC or other additives can act as strong microwave receptors: <cite id="5ebcdfa9-5">microwave absorbers can increase the temperature of the reaction by indirectly heating the surrounding particles of biomass</cite>, and <cite id="5ebcdfa9-7">SiC absorbent significantly enhances heating rate</cite>. Likewise, one review states that by exploiting <cite id="bfb566b8-4">the superior microwave absorbance of exogenous microwave absorbents and reaction catalysts, we can achieve very high heating rates</cite>.  

**Effect on heating behavior:** faster and more effective microwave coupling generally gives higher heating rates, better temperature rise, and often more uniform/controllable pyrolysis conditions, which can raise throughput and stabilize product formation. In short, absorbents mainly solve the **energy-transfer problem**.

**Catalysts mainly affect product selectivity.** Reviews report that microwave catalytic pyrolysis aims at both <cite id="5ebcdfa9-0">efficient heating of biomass and improving the selectivity of target products</cite>. The catalyst can strongly change the product slate: <cite id="5ebcdfa9-2">the addition of proper catalysts to a microwave pyrolysis process can dramatically influence the process' product selectivity</cite>. Catalytic upgrading of vapors is also used <cite id="5ebcdfa9-8">to obtain adequate process selectivity in respect of the product</cite>. Reported effects include upgrading oxygen-rich bio-oil by deoxygenation/cracking/aromatization; for example, catalyst-assisted microwave heating gave <cite id="bfb566b8-6">higher aromatic hydrocarbon yield, lower oxygen content and high heating value of bio-oil</cite>.

So, practically:

- **Absorbents** → better microwave coupling, faster heating, higher temperatures, often improved conversion and bio-oil yield/quality.
- **Catalysts** → altered reaction pathways and vapor upgrading, shifting yields among gas/liquid/char and often favoring better-quality liquids such as more aromatics and fewer oxygenates.

Overall, microwave catalytic pyrolysis is valued because it combines <cite id="5ebcdfa9-3">efficient heating of biomass</cite> with <cite id="5ebcdfa9-3">improving the selectivity of target products</cite>.

During gas conditioning for methanation, the WGS step is used when the raw syngas is too CO-rich: <cite id="4357ffa0-3">methanation consumes three molecules of H2 for each CO molecule</cite> and <cite id="4357ffa0-3">the H2/CO ratio in the product gas can be about 1:1</cite>, so operators apply WGS, <cite id="72c0150f-2">CO + H2O = CO2 + H2</cite>, because it is <cite id="72c0150f-2">the most used method to increase the hydrogen content in syngas</cite> and <cite id="4357ffa0-1">shifts a portion of the CO in syngas to CO2 and additional H2</cite>. The shift is enhanced mainly by adding more steam: <cite id="72c0150f-2">with the increase in the H2O/...</cite> ratio WGS is driven toward more hydrogen production, <cite id="5eb91bc6-0">steam addition improves conversion by shifting the reaction toward products</cite>, and <cite id="5eb91bc6-3">increasing steam flow rate increases H2 yield while suppressing CH4 and coke formation</cite>. Industrially, this upgrading is further improved by reactor/catalyst design, because <cite id="20251f72-1">CO is reacted downstream in two, high- and low-temperature, water-gas-shift reactors to further generate H2 and CO2</cite>, and <cite id="5eb91bc6-6">sulfur-tolerant WGS catalysts have been developed for operation under low steam/gas ratio conditions</cite>.

<cite id="2856506e-2">Using vacuum at high reaction temperature increased the glycerol conversion by eliminating the formed water from the reaction medium and led to a narrowing of the molecular weight distribution.</cite>

So, in practical terms: <cite id="2856506e-2">vacuum plus high temperature increases conversion</cite> because <cite id="2856506e-2">it removes the water produced during polymerization</cite>, and it also <cite id="2856506e-2">narrows the molecular weight distribution</cite> rather than broadening it.

In oxidation reactions over carbonate-forming metal catalysts, CO2 often has a <cite id="69853db7-0">negative effect on catalytic efficiency because adding CO2 reduces the oxidation rate and selectivity, and deactivation is accelerated due to increased carbonate formation on the catalyst surface.</cite> This means product yields for the desired oxidation product can fall when CO2 blocks or poisons active sites via surface carbonates <cite id="69853db7-0">reducing the CO oxidation rate and the selectivity</cite>. However, CO2 can also be beneficial in some oxidation systems used as a mild oxidant, where <cite id="69853db7-1">CO2 promotes selectivity by contaminating the non-selective species of several catalysts, preventing the production of several by-products.</cite> So, the overall effect is system-dependent: moderate CO2 can improve selectivity, but <cite id="fef0b422-0">a sharp reduction in product yield was observed ... at high pressure</cite>, and in many oxidation cases excess CO2 lowers activity by stabilizing surface carbonate species.

For biodiesel production, sodium methoxide is generally the better-performing catalyst, while sodium hydroxide is often simpler to buy and may look cheaper upfront.

- **Catalytic activity:** <cite id="f8ef4d7c-0">In transesterification, the active catalyst species is the methoxide radical (CH3O-), and catalyst activity depends on how much methoxide is available.</cite> Because sodium methoxide supplies that active species directly, <cite id="95d4236e-1">sodium methoxide exhibits superior catalytic activity</cite> relative to sodium hydroxide, which must first react with methanol to generate methoxide. <cite id="55fedfdb-0">When sodium hydroxide is dissolved in methanol, it creates the needed methoxide ion but also creates water.</cite>

- **Yield / soap formation:** Sodium methoxide usually gives better effective yield because it causes less soap-related loss. <cite id="f8ef4d7c-0">Methoxides do not eliminate soap formation, especially with free fatty acids present, but they cause less saponification of esters or triglycerides than KOH and NaOH.</cite> A recent review likewise states that <cite id="95d4236e-1">sodium methoxide shows superior yield performance with reduced soap formation.</cite> This matters because <cite id="95d4236e-5">soap formation decreases biodiesel yield selectivity, inhibits ester/glycerol separation, and forms emulsions.</cite>

- **Cost:** Sodium hydroxide often appears cheaper as a raw chemical, but sodium methoxide can be competitive or even cheaper in practice. <cite id="55fedfdb-0">Sodium methylate solutions appear more expensive than sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide, but can be less expensive in practice.</cite> The same source explains why: <cite id="55fedfdb-0">the methoxide solution already contains methanol, less sodium methylate may be needed than sodium hydroxide for the same extent of reaction, and extra soap from hydroxide use raises downstream processing costs.</cite>

- **Practical considerations:**  
  - **Water sensitivity / feedstock quality:** <cite id="55fedfdb-0">Using sodium hydroxide to make methoxide generates water, and water causes soap formation through saponification.</cite> Also, <cite id="95d4236e-4">sodium methoxide demands dry conditions, and water or high FFA can cause soap formation and yield loss.</cite> So neither catalyst is ideal for wet or high-FFA feedstocks without pretreatment, though sodium methoxide avoids adding water itself.  
  - **Commercial use:** <cite id="55fedfdb-0">Commercial producers prefer sodium methoxide solutions already dissolved in methanol</cite> because they are made by a <cite id="55fedfdb-0">water-free process so the catalyst does not contribute to soap formation.</cite>  
  - **Safety / handling:** Sodium methoxide has more severe handling issues. <cite id="123c2328-7">Sodium methoxide is violently water reactive and toxic, and powdered methoxides are a dust explosion hazard.</cite> Another safety source notes <cite id="123c2328-6">it reacts violently with water and is highly flammable.</cite>

**Bottom line:** <cite id="95d4236e-1">Sodium methoxide generally offers higher catalytic activity and better yield with less soap formation</cite>, making it preferred in industrial biodiesel plants, especially with dry, low-FFA feedstocks. But <cite id="55fedfdb-0">sodium hydroxide can look cheaper upfront</cite> and is commonly used by smaller producers, even though <cite id="55fedfdb-0">it generates water during catalyst preparation</cite> and often increases soap-related losses and cleanup burden.

During biomass hydrothermal liquefaction, <cite id="d3475a3d-3,c34aae4d-3">increasing residence time generally increases bio-oil yield at first and reduces solid residue/char, because conversion proceeds further</cite>. However, <cite id="d3475a3d-3">bio-oil often reaches a maximum at an intermediate time (for example, 15 min in one reviewed case), while the solid residue can decrease initially and then rise again at longer times</cite>, consistent with secondary reactions. For gas, the available evidence here indicates the opposite trend to oil at short times: <cite id="f1479479-0">decreasing reaction time enhanced gas yield while decreasing bio-oil production</cite>. So, in short, <cite id="d3475a3d-3,c34aae4d-3,f1479479-0">longer residence time tends to favor liquid formation and reduce solids initially, but excessive time can lower the bio-oil optimum and may increase secondary solid/gas formation, whereas shorter times tend to give more gas and less bio-oil</cite>.

The <cite id="30fa1e16-0,30fa1e16-4,30fa1e16-7">main factor is the feedstock’s free fatty acid (FFA) content, because FFAs react differently with acid and base catalysts.</cite>

- For <cite id="30fa1e16-4,30fa1e16-7">low-FFA oils</cite>, producers typically favor <cite id="d673bd84-0">base-catalyzed transesterification because acid catalysts are slower and require longer reaction times.</cite>
- For <cite id="30fa1e16-4,30fa1e16-7">high-FFA oils</cite>, a base catalyst is usually avoided at first because <cite id="30fa1e16-4,30fa1e16-7">high FFA leads to soap formation (saponification), causing emulsions, difficult phase separation, and loss of effective catalyst.</cite>
- Therefore, for high-FFA feedstocks, the usual order is <cite id="30fa1e16-0,30fa1e16-6">first acid-catalyzed esterification to reduce FFAs, then base-catalyzed transesterification.</cite> This is done because <cite id="30fa1e16-0">the first-stage acid esterification lowers FFA levels and prevents soap formation in the subsequent base-catalyzed step.</cite>

So, catalyst selection and sequence are determined mainly by:
1. <cite id="30fa1e16-0,30fa1e16-4">FFA level in the oil</cite>  
2. <cite id="30fa1e16-4,30fa1e16-7">risk of soap formation with alkali catalysts</cite>  
3. <cite id="d673bd84-0">reaction-rate tradeoff: acids can handle FFAs but are slower; bases are faster but require low FFA feedstocks</cite>

In short: <cite id="d673bd84-0,30fa1e16-0,30fa1e16-6">low-FFA oils usually go directly to base transesterification, while high-FFA oils are treated first with acid esterification and then with base transesterification.</cite>

Copper ions catalyze H₂O₂ decomposition through a <cite id="4cf87b26-3">circular redox reaction between Cu(II) and Cu(I)</cite>. In this cycle, <cite id="4cf87b26-4">ascorbic acid reduces copper to the cuprous form</cite> and <cite id="4cf87b26-0">does so via consecutive one-electron oxidations</cite>, producing ascorbyl/dehydroascorbate-type oxidation products. The reduced metal then reacts with peroxide: <cite id="02210ce4-8">Cu(I) and H₂O₂ form hydroxyl radical</cite>, and this is part of <cite id="02210ce4-2">Fenton-like copper redox chemistry</cite>. The resulting oxidation of Cu(I) back to Cu(II) lets ascorbate reduce it again, so copper is regenerated and repeatedly accelerates peroxide breakdown. In short, the net mechanism is: <cite id="4cf87b26-4">ascorbate → Cu(II) to Cu(I)</cite>, then <cite id="02210ce4-8">Cu(I) + H₂O₂ → reactive radicals + Cu(II)</cite>, with continuous redox cycling driving catalytic H₂O₂ decomposition.

In CO₂ methanation, increasing the H₂/CO₂ ratio generally raises methane yield because the Sabatier stoichiometric requirement is 4:1 and H₂-rich feeds push the reaction toward CH₄ formation. In the calculation, the molar ratio of nCO2:nH2 = 1:4 was used as the condition for the stoichiometric ratio in the methanation reaction. At the higher H2:CO2 ratio of 4:1, the results show a higher CO2 conversion and high methane yield. More specifically, when the H2:CO2 ratio was increased from 2:1 to 4:1, the results show a higher CO2 conversion and high methane yield. A lower ratio tends to leave the system H₂-limited, reducing methane production; one source notes that the H2/CO ratio should not be less than 3 to obtain a high methane yield. For selectivity, a higher H₂/CO₂ ratio usually improves CH₄ selectivity by suppressing competing CO formation via the reverse water-gas shift pathway. This is consistent with the broader finding that the thermodynamic analysis of CO2 methanation emphasizes the significant impact of temperature, pressure, and the H2/CO2 molar ratio on both CH4 yield and CO2 conversion and with comparative reaction studies showing ratio-dependent tuning between RWGS and methanation products. variations in the feed gas stream (H2:CO2 ratio) can affect product distribution, and in contrast RWGS-oriented systems often favor lower effective H₂ excess for CO production rather than CH₄. Stoichimetically, the RWGS should be successfully accomplished when the H2/CO2 ratio is 1. However, a higher H2/CO2 ratio is more favoured when it comes to the ... So, in practical terms: - Around H₂/CO₂ = 4:1 is the stoichiometric target for methanation. - Below that, methane yield drops when the ratio is too low (especially below ~3). - Raising the ratio toward 4:1 typically increases CO₂ conversion and CH₄ yield. - Beyond stoichiometric excess, gains often diminish and the benefit becomes process-specific rather than fundamental. So the short answer is: higher H₂/CO₂ ratios, up to about the stoichiometric 4:1 level, generally increase methane yield and usually improve methane selectivity; lower ratios reduce CH₄ formation and favor more incomplete conversion or competing CO formation.

On iron-containing CWPO catalysts, the **surface iron oxidation state controls how efficiently H₂O₂ is activated into oxidizing radicals**. In heterogeneous Fenton/CWPO chemistry, **surface Fe(II) is the more active site for H₂O₂ decomposition**, and **regeneration of Fe(II) from Fe(III)** is important because it sustains the redox cycle that produces radicals. Evidence from the literature shows that <cite id="4ae81a2c-0">reducing Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ on the goethite surface increased catalytic efficiency</cite>, and that <cite id="4ae81a2c-5">promoting the reduction of Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ on the catalyst surface increased the oxidation rate because H₂O₂ decomposition was enhanced</cite>. More broadly, the review notes that <cite id="e70be6aa-0">incorporation of semiconductor material improves the rate of regeneration of Fe(II) from Fe(III)</cite>, which is mechanistically important for maintaining activity.

The **amount and distribution of Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ surface species also affect hydroxyl-radical generation directly**. One study snippet reports that a catalyst with a <cite id="d86ea4fe-0">Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ratio of 1.29</cite> and that <cite id="d86ea4fe-0">heterogeneous Fenton reaction was proved by surface-Fe and radical ·OH radicals analysis</cite>. This supports the idea that the **surface redox pair Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ is not passive**; it is the catalytic cycle through which H₂O₂ is converted to reactive species such as ·OH.

These iron species influence **overall CWPO efficiency** in two main ways:

1. **Positive effect when the surface promotes productive H₂O₂ activation**  
   Catalysts with accessible iron sites, good electron transfer, and support structures that stabilize/disperse iron tend to work better because <cite id="e70be6aa-0">iron minerals supported on clay materials, perovskites, carbon materials, zeolites and metal-organic frameworks dramatically increase the catalytic degradation rate of contaminants by providing high surface area, good mechanical stability, and improved electron transfer</cite>. Also, in Fe/AC systems, <cite id="4ae81a2c-1">adsorbed phenol on catalyst surface</cite> led to <cite id="4ae81a2c-1">a better use of the oxidant</cite>, showing that surface iron sites are more effective when pollutant adsorption and radical formation occur close together.

2. **Negative effect when iron is lost, blocked, or shifts into less active forms**  
   CWPO efficiency declines if iron leaches from the surface or if deposits/passivation hinder access to active sites. For example, <cite id="4ae81a2c-2">increased leaching of the iron</cite> was associated with reduced mineralization, and <cite id="4ae81a2c-6">the surface hindered the activity of the Fe/γ-Al2O3 catalyst</cite>. In practice, this means that not only the presence of iron, but its **surface speciation, accessibility, and stability**, determine performance.

So, in concise terms: **surface Fe²⁺ sites are key for generating hydroxyl radicals from H₂O₂, Fe³⁺ must be efficiently reduced back to Fe²⁺ to sustain the cycle, and catalyst efficiency is highest when iron remains well-dispersed, accessible, and resistant to leaching/passivation.** When that balance is optimized, CWPO achieves faster oxidation and better oxidant utilization; when it is not, radical production and pollutant mineralization drop.

Potassium acts as a <cite id="e9734150-5">content-dependent promoter whose loading can change catalytic activity</cite> and <cite id="e9734150-5">phase composition</cite>. On iron catalysts, <cite id="bc8638ca-0">increasing K loading can make activity decrease, pass through a maximum, or increase</cite>, but <cite id="0034ac08-1,9f6e25b4-1">higher potassium loading is also reported to lower catalytic activity</cite>; at the same time, <cite id="9f6e25b4-7">changing K content causes very pronounced changes in selectivity to C2+ hydrocarbons</cite>. On Ni catalysts, <cite id="0034ac08-5">a low K amount (1.6 wt.%) gave high stability</cite>, while <cite id="bc8638ca-7">an intermediate loading (7%Ni–1%K2O) showed the highest activity</cite>, indicating an optimum rather than “more K is always better.” On Pt catalysts, <cite id="85e38e01-0">controlled addition of potassium was beneficial for both activity and selectivity</cite>, and <cite id="85e38e01-8">K promotion has been linked to electron transfer from Pt to O in KO</cite>. In Cu-based systems, <cite id="9f6e25b4-0">potassium boosts electrostatic interactions, facilitates electron transfer, and increases CO2 adsorption capacity</cite>. Co-based catalysts show the strongest reaction dependence: <cite id="85e38e01-4">K addition increased C5+ and CO2 selectivity and decreased CH4 selectivity</cite> in Fischer–Tropsch-related work, <cite id="0034ac08-9">its promoter effect increased as KOH quantity increased on Co/silicate catalysts</cite>, yet <cite id="85e38e01-1">potassium was detrimental to catalytic activity for ammonia synthesis on cobalt catalysts</cite>. Overall, <cite id="bc8638ca-1,0034ac08-1,0034ac08-5,85e38e01-0">low or controlled K loadings often improve activity/selectivity or stability, whereas excessive K can reduce activity or stability, so the optimal potassium content is strongly metal- and reaction-specific</cite>.

3D DIC combines <cite id="9adc32e4-2">image-based coordinate recovery</cite> with <cite id="9adc32e4-0">stereo-correlation of subsets, and stereo-triangulation</cite> to measure how an object’s surface moves and deforms.

In practice, the object surface is given a random speckle pattern, and two calibrated cameras view it from different angles. DIC then <cite id="9adc32e4-9">tracks the movement of the naturally occurring or applied surface pattern during the test or experiment</cite> by following small pixel subsets between images. Because the same subset is seen by both cameras, the system can use <cite id="9adc32e4-0">stereo-triangulation</cite> to reconstruct that subset’s 3D position from the two lines of sight, which is the core photogrammetry step. More generally, <cite id="9adc32e4-2">Digital Image Correlation (DIC) is a procedure to compute 2D or 3D coordinates from recorded single images or image series</cite>.

Once the surface points are reconstructed before and after loading, 3D DIC compares their 3D coordinates over time to obtain full-field displacement; spatial gradients of that displacement field give strain and deformation. This is why <cite id="9adc32e4-0">3D DIC obtains full-field 3D shape, deformation</cite>, and related quantities, and why systems can achieve high precision by <cite id="9adc32e4-7">tracking the same patterned subset region across stereo image sequences</cite>.

So, in one sentence: 3D DIC uses photogrammetry to reconstruct 3D surface points from synchronized stereo images, and triangulation to locate each tracked surface subset in space before and after deformation, allowing full-field displacement and strain measurement.

Organic solvent additives generally shift vaterite precipitation by changing both **how fast CaCO₃ forms** and **which polymorph/morphology is favored**.

- **Nucleation / precipitation rate:** Studies report that <cite id="df22cfec-1">the presence of an organic additive influenced the precipitation rate</cite>. More specifically, alcohol-type additives can accelerate/selectively favor vaterite formation; for example, <cite id="1471f0cc-0">IPA mediates the rapid and selective synthesis of vaterite in aqueous solution</cite>. In practice, this means solvent additives can alter the effective supersaturation/solvation environment enough to change the onset and pathway of nucleation.

- **Growth and polymorph selection:** Organic solvents can increase the amount of vaterite obtained during precipitation. The solvent-additive study found that <cite id="df22cfec-1">the presence of an organic additive influenced ... the content of vaterite in the obtained product</cite>. Reviews also note that <cite id="9870c987-4">some additives, e.g., ethylene glycol, can promote vaterite formation</cite>. So, these additives do not just change nucleation timing; they also steer subsequent crystal growth toward the metastable vaterite phase rather than calcite/aragonite.

- **Morphology:** Solvent additives also affect particle shape and surface structure. The same precipitation study states that <cite id="df22cfec-1">the presence of an organic additive influenced ... the morphology</cite>, and another source notes that <cite id="9870c987-2">these additives influence the morphology of the vaterite crystals formed</cite>. In other words, solvents can change whether vaterite appears as more spherical, spherulitic, porous, or otherwise differently aggregated particles by modifying growth rates on different crystal faces and aggregation behavior.

- **Stability / transformation:** Vaterite is inherently metastable, and solvent additives often help preserve it. Vaterite itself is <cite id="9870c987-0">a metastable polymorph of calcium carbonate</cite>. Yet solvent/additive studies report that <cite id="9870c987-2">these additives ... stabilize this mineral phase by preventing the transformation to calcite</cite>. Consistently, ethylene glycol has been reported such that <cite id="df22cfec-7">60% EG concentration prevents vaterite/aragonite-to-calcite transformation</cite>. So additives can prolong vaterite lifetime by slowing the usual dissolution–reprecipitation route to calcite.

Overall: organic solvents such as ethanol, isopropanol, diethylene glycol, and ethylene glycol tend to **modify nucleation kinetics, favor vaterite during growth, reshape particle morphology, and retard conversion to calcite**. **Key methodology**
- Use a crystallization route that promotes <cite id="23bf1211-0,b8bbd23b-0">spherulitic growth</cite> rather than faceted crystal growth.
- In calcium citrate specifically, the review reports that <cite id="810289ca-0,23bf1211-3">factors affecting the shape of calcium citrate during reactive crystallization include supersaturation and shear stress.</cite>
- The same review notes that, from the shear-stress analysis, the main practical operating levers for morphology were <cite id="b8bbd23b-3,23bf1211-3">stirring rate and residence time</cite>, and that this approach was <cite id="b8bbd23b-3">successfully scaled up</cite>.

**Most important control parameters**
1. **Supersaturation**
   - This is a primary driver of calcium citrate shape formation: <cite id="810289ca-0,23bf1211-3">factors affecting the shape of calcium citrate during reactive crystallization include supersaturation</cite>.
   - Industrially, this means controlling feed concentration, dosing rate, local mixing, and pH/composition trajectory so nucleation and growth favor aggregate/spherulite formation rather than elongated or irregular crystals.

2. **Shear stress / mixing intensity**
   - The review explicitly identifies <cite id="810289ca-0,23bf1211-3">shear stress</cite> as shape-controlling.
   - In practice, shear is most directly tuned through <cite id="b8bbd23b-3,23bf1211-3">stirring rate</cite>. Too little or too much shear can change aggregation, breakage, and radial growth behavior.

3. **Residence time**
   - Calcium citrate spherulites require enough time to develop; <cite id="810289ca-1,810289ca-3,b8bbd23b-0">temperature, stirring rate, and residence time were critical parameters for regulating the spherulite shape and size.</cite>
   - Residence time is therefore a scale-up-critical variable in MSMPR or continuous reactors, and also matters in batch hold/aging stages.

4. **Temperature**
   - The same calcium citrate spherulite study found that <cite id="810289ca-1,810289ca-3,b8bbd23b-0">temperature ... [is a] critical parameter for regulating the spherulite shape and size.</cite>
   - Temperature affects solubility, supersaturation profile, growth rate, and likely the balance between faceted growth and spherulitic aggregation.

**Industrial takeaway**
A practical recipe for spherical calcium citrate is to design the process around <cite id="23bf1211-0,b8bbd23b-0">spherulitic growth</cite> and then optimize the coupled set of <cite id="810289ca-0,23bf1211-3">supersaturation and shear stress</cite> variables, with <cite id="810289ca-1,810289ca-3,b8bbd23b-3">temperature, stirring rate, and residence time</cite> as the main operating knobs. During nanoindentation, grain boundaries (GBs) affect plasticity mainly by changing <cite id="c33a78f9-0">when and where dislocations nucleate</cite> and by controlling whether they are <cite id="8d20ee4f-1">blocked, absorbed, transmitted, or emitted</cite>. The result is that the first “pop-in” event, the size of the plastically affected zone, and the measured hardness can all change strongly near a boundary. <cite id="8d20ee4f-0">Grain boundaries, free surfaces, and pre-existing dislocations can facilitate dislocation nucleation under local stress concentration, thereby lowering the pop-in stress</cite>; in some cases, <cite id="8d20ee4f-0">nanoindentation near a grain boundary can also lead to a two-stage pop-in phenomenon, likely associated with dislocation nucleation and penetration through the grain boundary.</cite>

More specifically, GB characteristics matter in several ways:

- **Boundary character and structure:** <cite id="8d20ee4f-1">Reported dislocation–GB interaction modes include blockage, absorption, transmission, and emission, governed by GB structure, slip geometry, and local stress state.</cite>
- **Misorientation / angle:** <cite id="8d20ee4f-8">The critical resolved shear stress for dislocation transmission across an α-Fe grain boundary increases with increasing grain boundary energy and grain misorientation.</cite> Consistently, <cite id="8d20ee4f-5">low-angle grain boundaries can act as easier pathways for dislocation transmission than high-angle boundaries</cite>, and in Al/Cu <cite id="8d20ee4f-5">symmetric and asymmetric tilt low-angle boundaries showed less resistance to transmission than twist low-angle boundaries.</cite>
- **Indent distance from the GB:** in Ni, <cite id="8d20ee4f-2">the size and location of the initial dislocation embryos varied with the distance between the indenter and the GB.</cite>

Across **different metals**, the balance between softening by easier nucleation and hardening by dislocation blockage differs:

- **BCC metals (Fe, Mo, W):** experiments/review show strong near-GB effects. In α-Fe, <cite id="8d20ee4f-1">the initial plasticity beneath the indenter was found to be caused by collective dislocation emission at the GB and in the grain interior, with the GB-mediated process requiring less energy.</cite> In Mo, <cite id="8d20ee4f-1">the transition from source exhaustion to forest hardening was delayed near the GB because mobile dislocations were blocked by the boundary.</cite> In W, <cite id="8d20ee4f-1"><111> screw dislocations were observed to transmit from the soft grain into the hard grain across the GB under nanoindentation.</cite> Also, the spatial extent differs by metal: <cite id="8d20ee4f-3">in Fe–14%Si, the contribution of the grain boundary to the incipient plasticity was confined to a zone of about 10 nm from the boundary, whereas in Mo a more extensive affected zone of about 35 nm was found.</cite>
- **FCC metals (Cu, Ni, Al):** GBs often both assist nucleation and obstruct glide. In bicrystal Cu, <cite id="8d20ee4f-0">a pre-existing grain boundary was reported to significantly reduce the critical stress for dislocation nucleation due to stress concentration.</cite> In polycrystalline Ni, <cite id="8d20ee4f-2">the grain boundary not only promoted the onset of plasticity but also blocked dislocation glide, resulting in more dislocation locks and debris.</cite> Thus <cite id="8d20ee4f-2">by impeding dislocation motion, the grain boundary strengthened the material and increased local hardness.</cite> More broadly for nanocrystalline Al and Cu, <cite id="8d20ee4f-6">grain boundaries both emit and absorb dislocations while also contributing to strengthening through impeded dislocation motion and pile-up effects.</cite>

This is why nanoindentation hardness near a GB is often **non-monotonic** rather than simply higher or lower. In interstitial-free steel, <cite id="8d20ee4f-4">nanohardness near the grain boundary was slightly lower than in the grain interior at shallow penetration, but became higher at larger penetration depths.</cite> The proposed reason was that <cite id="8d20ee4f-4">geometrically necessary dislocations initially accumulated at the grain boundary beneath the indenter, while larger plastic zones at greater depth generated enough dislocations to activate sources in the adjacent grain; this collective dislocation emission increased resistance to deformation and raised hardness near the boundary.</cite> Likewise, in Fe–14%Si and Mo, <cite id="8d20ee4f-3">regions of increased hardness adjacent to the grain boundaries were identified after initial softening</cite>, and <cite id="8d20ee4f-3">the increased hardness was attributed to geometrically necessary dislocations and/or dislocations left behind after repulsion by the grain boundary.</cite>

So, in one sentence: **grain boundaries can make nanoindentation plasticity start earlier by aiding dislocation nucleation, but then often make continued plastic flow harder by trapping, blocking, or redirecting dislocations; the exact outcome depends on boundary type, misorientation, slip geometry, indenter distance, and the metal’s crystal structure.** <cite id="8d20ee4f-1">Distinct mechanisms have been observed depending on GB type and metal</cite>.

In starch-based edible films, the effect on tensile strength and flexibility depends on whether the added component acts mainly as a reinforcer or a plasticizer/disruptor. - Blending starch with other biopolymers such as chitosan and PVA can enhance flexibility. - Adding chitosan generally improves mechanical strength: chitosan concentration positively affects elastic modulus and tensile strength. - Some starch-based composite blends can improve both tensile strength and elongation at break, meaning the right blend can make films both stronger and less brittle. - By contrast, plasticizers such as glycerol significantly increase film flexibility, but glycerol mainly enhances elongation at break and can negatively impact mechanical properties, so films usually become more stretchable but less strong/stiff. - Essential oils often lower tensile strength while increasing elongation at break, which again reflects a trade-off toward greater flexibility and lower resistance to pulling forces. Overall: stronger/stiffer starch films are usually obtained by reinforcing blends such as chitosan-containing systems, while more flexible/stretchable films are usually obtained with plasticizers like glycerol or certain essential oils, often at the cost of tensile strength.

Semantic segmentation methods for brain tumor MRI usually handle resolution loss from repeated down-sampling by combining several design choices:

1. <cite id="572e4d35-0">Encoder–decoder networks with skip connections</cite>. The basic idea is to pass high-resolution features from early encoder layers directly to the decoder, so boundary/detail information lost during pooling can be reused during up-sampling. This is a common reason U-Net-style models work well in tumor MRI. More directly, <cite id="7f0a9f36-3">“although skip connections help recover spatial information” in the up-sampling phase</cite>, and <cite id="7f0a9f36-7">3D U-Net variants often use multiple skip connections</cite> to strengthen this recovery.

2. <cite id="572e4d35-3">Dilated convolution</cite> to enlarge the receptive field without further reducing feature-map resolution. In brain tumor segmentation, surveys note that <cite id="572e4d35-9">skip connections and dilated convolution residual blocks are combined to improve the network’s ability to identify tumor features more accurately</cite>. This helps preserve localization while still capturing larger tumor context.

3. <cite id="7f0a9f36-0,7f0a9f36-1,7f0a9f36-2">Multi-scale feature extraction and fusion</cite>. Since tumors vary in size and shape, models aggregate features from several scales so coarse semantic context and fine spatial detail are both available to the decoder. Multi-scale attention U-Net and dual-stream multi-scale 3D U-Net variants are examples of this strategy in brain tumor MRI.

4. <cite id="7f0a9f36-0,7f0a9f36-5">Attention mechanisms</cite>. Attention helps the network emphasize informative regions/features when reconstructing the segmentation mask, which can sharpen tumor boundaries and suppress irrelevant background after resolution has been reduced in deeper layers.

5. <cite id="572e4d35-2">Alternative down-sampling schemes that preserve detail better, such as wavelet-based downsampling</cite>. These approaches explicitly try to retain frequency/detail information during the encoder’s reduction stages, reducing the amount of spatial information lost in the first place.

So, in short: brain tumor MRI segmentation addresses down-sampling loss mainly through <cite id="572e4d35-0,7f0a9f36-3">skip-connected encoder–decoder reconstruction</cite>, <cite id="572e4d35-3,572e4d35-9">dilated convolutions</cite>, <cite id="7f0a9f36-0,7f0a9f36-1,7f0a9f36-2">multi-scale fusion</cite>, <cite id="7f0a9f36-0,7f0a9f36-5">attention</cite>, and sometimes <cite id="572e4d35-2">detail-preserving down-sampling such as wavelets</cite>. These methods let the model recover fine tumor boundaries while still benefiting from deep, context-rich features.

The PECVD method for TiO₂ deposition uses the same core hardware as other plasma-assisted CVD systems, with Ti-containing and oxidizing precursors added for the specific film chemistry.

**Main components**
- A **vacuum reaction chamber** where deposition occurs under reduced pressure; PECVD is described as a <cite id="02d0ae37-1">low temperature vacuum deposition process</cite>.
- A **gas/precursor delivery system** that feeds vapor-phase reactants into the chamber; in CVD/PECVD, <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">gas phase constituents react at a surface to be deposited</cite>.
- A **plasma generation system**, usually **RF powered electrodes**, because <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">the well established technology of PECVD uses RF power source to excite plasma</cite>.
- A **substrate holder/heater**, since TiO₂ films by RF-PECVD have been grown at <cite id="02d0ae37-0">substrate temperatures between 393 and 523 K</cite>.
- A **vacuum pumping / pressure-control system** to maintain the low-pressure plasma environment implied by the process being a <cite id="02d0ae37-1">low temperature vacuum deposition process</cite> and by the chamber/reactor configuration in PECVD systems <cite id="02d0ae37-7">reaction chamber, gas delivery, vacuum, and plasma generation</cite>.

**Operating principle**
- In ordinary CVD, film growth relies on thermal activation because <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">the gas phase constituents react at a surface to be deposited</cite> and <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">the process is limited by the substrate temperature which is the only source of energy to promote surface chemistry</cite>.
- In PECVD, a plasma is created from the reactant gases. This plasma activates and dissociates the precursor molecules, so deposition can proceed at lower temperature: <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">PECVD offers enhanced deposition rates at reduced substrate temperature since the reactants are in the form of plasma</cite> and <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">energetic electrons in the plasma activate the CVD process as opposed to thermal energy associated with conventional CVD</cite>.
- The activated species then reach the substrate and react there to form the thin film. For TiO₂ PECVD specifically, this means plasma-activated Ti-containing precursor fragments react with oxygen-containing species at the substrate surface to build the oxide film.
- PECVD reactors can be **direct** or **remote**: in direct PECVD, <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">the substrate is also immersed within plasma</cite>; in remote PECVD, <cite id="1d1b1bf0-0">active species are extracted and transported to a plasma free region</cite> where deposition occurs on a heated substrate.

So, in short: PECVD for TiO₂ consists mainly of a **vacuum chamber, precursor gas delivery, RF plasma source/electrodes, substrate heater/holder, and pumping/pressure controls**, and it works by using **plasma-generated reactive species to drive TiO₂ film formation at lower temperatures than conventional thermal CVD**. <cite id="02d0ae37-0,02d0ae37-1,1d1b1bf0-0"> </cite>
