## How exercise lowers HbA1c in T2DM

Exercise improves HbA1c in type 2 diabetes mainly by <cite id="2a61780d-0">improving HbA1c, fasting and postprandial glucose levels, insulin sensitivity, and fasting insulin levels</cite>. Mechanistically, this happens through repeated acute glucose-lowering effects during each exercise bout, plus longer-lasting adaptations in skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue that make the body more insulin-sensitive. Those benefits are not fleeting: <cite id="43925f6a-0">all exercise conditions improved SI for at least 48 hours</cite>, and in adults with T2DM <cite id="43925f6a-1">this may persist beyond 72 hours after the last exercise session</cite>.

### 1) Acute muscle contraction increases glucose uptake even when insulin action is impaired
A central mechanism is skeletal muscle glucose disposal, because <cite id="65d1c055-1">skeletal muscle is responsible for around 80% of insulin-stimulated glucose disposal</cite>. During exercise, <cite id="65d1c055-0">both insulin and exercise increase skeletal muscle glucose uptake by translocation of glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4)</cite>, and importantly <cite id="2b983af9-1">acute exercise induces GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle of normal human subjects and subjects with type 2 diabetes</cite>. This helps patients with T2DM because <cite id="2b983af9-8">exercise activates molecular signals that bypass defects in insulin action in skeletal muscle</cite>, and <cite id="2b983af9-0">GLUT4 translocation during exercise is normal in skeletal muscle of type 2 diabetics</cite>.

### 2) Contraction-triggered biochemical signaling drives this uptake
The biochemical trigger is the energetic stress of contraction. During exercise, <cite id="2b983af9-4">energy expenditure in skeletal muscle</cite> rises, causing <cite id="2b983af9-4">an elevated ratio of AMP/- to ADP/ATP</cite>, and <cite id="2b983af9-6">an acute bout of exercise leads to a significant increase in AMPK α2 activity in the skeletal muscle</cite>. Reviews therefore conclude that <cite id="2b983af9-3">exercise increases glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity of skeletal muscle and these effects are primarily mediated by increased GLUT4 translocation</cite>. More recent work also reports that <cite id="65443c6e-1">exercise training can enhance the induction of GLUT4 to AMPK, improve insulin signaling ability, increase nitric oxide (NO) synthesis</cite>.

### 3) Repeated training remodels muscle to become more insulin-sensitive
With regular training, the muscle becomes better equipped to remove glucose from blood. <cite id="65d1c055-5">Exercise training is the most potent stimulus to increase skeletal muscle GLUT4 expression</cite>, and <cite id="65443c6e-2">exercise training results in increased skeletal muscle mitochondria and GLUT4 protein expression</cite>. Consistent with that, <cite id="c6c0b14e-9">short-term aerobic exercise training improves insulin sensitivity in adults with T2D, paralleling improved mitochondrial function</cite>. These adaptations reduce glycemia not just during exercise, but between exercise sessions as well.

### 4) Exercise improves liver insulin sensitivity and suppresses excess hepatic glucose output
HbA1c also falls because exercise improves hepatic glucose regulation. In patients with T2D, <cite id="c6c0b14e-0">exercise training is known to diminish IHL and hepatic insulin resistance</cite>, thereby <cite id="c6c0b14e-0">enhancing insulin mediated suppression of HGP</cite>. High-intensity interval training similarly <cite id="c6c0b14e-4">lowers blood glucose levels by improving adipose and liver insulin sensitivity independently of changes in adiposity</cite>. This is especially relevant for fasting glucose, which contributes strongly to overall glycemic exposure.

### 5) Anti-inflammatory and oxidative-stress effects further improve insulin action
Exercise does not act only through glucose transport; it also changes the inflammatory and redox environment that drives insulin resistance. <cite id="2a61780d-2">Regular exercise induces anti-inflammatory responses, enhances antioxidant defenses, and promotes mitochondrial function, thereby improving insulin sensitivity</cite>. A related review likewise states that <cite id="c6c0b14e-1">regular exercise induces anti-inflammatory responses, enhances antioxidant defenses, and promotes mitochondrial function, thereby improving insulin sensitivity</cite>. These systemic effects help muscle, liver, and adipose tissue respond better to insulin.

### 6) Adipose-tissue adaptations may also contribute
Adipose tissue appears to adapt in ways that support better whole-body glucose handling. For example, <cite id="65443c6e-5">exercise training has been shown to increase adipose tissue GLUT4 content in type 2 diabetes</cite>. Combined with the liver and muscle effects above, that can reduce whole-body insulin resistance and improve average glucose exposure.

## Bottom line
In T2DM, exercise lowers HbA1c because it repeatedly increases contraction-mediated glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, improves post-exercise insulin sensitivity for <cite id="43925f6a-0">at least 48 hours</cite> and sometimes <cite id="43925f6a-1">beyond 72 hours</cite>, and over time increases <cite id="65d1c055-5">skeletal muscle GLUT4 expression</cite>, improves <cite id="c6c0b14e-9">mitochondrial function</cite>, reduces <cite id="c6c0b14e-0">hepatic insulin resistance</cite>, and promotes <cite id="2a61780d-2">anti-inflammatory responses</cite>. The integrated result is lower fasting and postprandial glucose and therefore better HbA1c control <cite id="2a61780d-0">across aerobic, resistance, and combined exercise modes</cite>.

To improve bone-health research in Turner syndrome (TS), the main priorities are better study design and more appropriate bone measurements.

**1) Use more standardized, less heterogeneous study cohorts.**  
A major problem is that existing TS studies are hard to compare because of <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">high heterogeneity among the subjects examined and the different methods applied to assess bone mineral status</cite>. Research should therefore define cohorts carefully by age, pubertal status, spontaneous vs induced puberty, and treatment exposure.

**2) Account explicitly for body size and short stature.**  
A key measurement issue is that <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">DXA may underestimate BMD in short children and adults because BMD is highly dependent on bone size</cite>. Since short stature is common in TS, studies should adjust areal BMD for body and bone size, and interpret DXA cautiously rather than treating raw DXA values as directly comparable to controls.

**3) Prefer methods that separate density from bone size and assess bone structure.**  
The review notes that <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">pQCT appears to be the only method able to distinguish between cortical and trabecular bone density, assess volumetric density independent of bone size, and evaluate bone geometry</cite>. That makes pQCT especially valuable in TS, where altered geometry and cortical thickness may contribute to fragility. Studies should include structural outcomes, not just areal BMD.

**4) Standardize and report hormone replacement therapy exposure in detail.**  
Interpretation of TS bone data is strongly confounded by estrogen treatment because <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">studies included subjects of different ages, with different percentages of spontaneous puberty and different duration of HRT, and used different dosages, timing, and formulations of estrogens</cite>. Also, <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">differences in BMD among studies may simply reflect the age at which HRT was initiated</cite>. Future studies should therefore measure and report age at HRT initiation, formulation, dose, route, duration, and cumulative exposure.

**5) Use longitudinal, prospective designs rather than mostly retrospective or cross-sectional work.**  
The evidence base on fractures is weak because <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">only few studies have assessed fracture rate in TS, with some including only adults and being retrospective</cite>. The review specifically concludes that <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">prospective studies are needed to identify risk factors for fractures in TS and to establish the real impact of osteoporosis</cite>. So stronger research should follow patients over time and include incident fracture outcomes.

**6) Include clinically relevant covariates beyond BMD.**  
Bone fragility in TS is not explained by one factor alone; contributing factors include <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">estrogen deficiency, altered bone geometry, reduced cortical thickness, and vitamin D deficiency</cite>. Better studies should therefore collect data on vitamin D, calcium intake, physical activity, GH treatment, and other endocrine factors rather than focusing only on densitometry.

**7) Power studies to examine genotype/karyotype effects.**  
Current evidence is inconclusive because <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">larger studies are needed to establish whether genotype can affect bone metabolism or fracture risk in TS</cite>. Multi-center cohorts would help address this.

In short, the best TS bone-health studies would be **prospective, longitudinal, and adequately powered; use standardized cohorts and detailed treatment characterization; adjust for short stature/body size; and incorporate volumetric/structural imaging such as pQCT alongside fracture outcomes** <cite id="0a9cf2e8-0">because methodological heterogeneity and size-dependent measurement bias currently limit conclusions</cite>.

Maternal micronutrient restriction appears to <cite id="4cf3ebb8-5">significantly increase the expression of leptin and 11β-HSD1 genes in offspring adipose tissue</cite>. More broadly, studies of maternal micronutrient deficiency report that <cite id="caedd846-1">leptin and 11βHSD1 genes in rat offspring were altered in B12 and Mg deficiency</cite>, and that these changes are linked to adiposity because <cite id="caedd846-4">increased expression of 11β-HSD1 and leptin may underlie enhanced body adiposity (fat percentage and visceral adiposity) in the offspring</cite>. Consistent with this, <cite id="100b7b6e-3">maternal vitamin and mineral restrictions both increased the offspring's body fat percentage, especially visceral fat</cite>. In short, maternal micronutrient restriction tends to program offspring toward a more adipogenic phenotype by upregulating or dysregulating genes such as 11β-HSD1 and leptin that promote fat accumulation.

Aspirin damages the gastric mucosal barrier by causing both a fall in mucosal potential difference and abnormal ion movement across the epithelium. Specifically, <cite id="486ebbe7-0">aspirin causes a significant fall in transmucosal potential difference (PD) across gastric mucosa of 15 mV</cite>, and <cite id="51e3d16d-6">luminal application of aspirin increases net cationic flux and reduces PD</cite>. These changes reflect barrier breakdown.

Functionally, the disrupted barrier allows <cite id="51e3d16d-3">hydrogen ion back-diffusion</cite> and is associated with altered sodium movement; in patients with barrier injury, <cite id="51e3d16d-7">H(+) flux out of the lumen and Na(+) flux into the lumen were significantly increased, indicating increased mucosal permeability</cite>. In other words, acid moves from the gastric lumen into the mucosa while sodium leaks in the opposite direction, showing loss of epithelial integrity.

This matters because the fall in PD is an electrical sign of increased permeability, and the abnormal ionic fluxes expose the mucosa to acid injury. Thus, aspirin-induced PD reduction and H+/Na+ flux abnormalities contribute to gastric damage by <cite id="486ebbe7-3">breaking the gastric mucosal barrier</cite>, which then permits acid-mediated epithelial injury and lesion formation.

Key features that matter for both diagnosis and prognosis of gastric volvulus are:

- **It is rare but potentially life-threatening.** <cite id="2af82b9b-0">Gastric volvulus is a rare clinical event in adult and pediatric patients</cite>, and <cite id="2af82b9b-0">gastric strangulation is a complication that can occur after the development of acute gastric volvulus</cite>. Prognosis improves because <cite id="2af82b9b-0">timely diagnosis and treatment of acute gastric volvulus can decrease morbidity and mortality</cite>.

- **Age and underlying anatomy strongly influence epidemiology.** It <cite id="8b53012a-2">has been reported in all age groups; however, it is typically diagnosed in the elderly</cite>. In adults, secondary volvulus is commonly linked to structural defects: <cite id="27b206b2-1">Paraesophageal hernia is the most common cause of secondary gastric volvulus in adults</cite>, and <cite id="27b206b2-3">secondary gastric volvulus is usually seen in the elderly and is nearly always associated with paraesophageal and diaphragmatic hernias</cite>.

- **Type of volvulus matters epidemiologically and clinically.** <cite id="8b53012a-2">Organo-axial volvulus is the most common type</cite>. Recognition of the axis of rotation is important because gastric volvulus occurs when the stomach <cite id="2af82b9b-0">rotates on itself at least 180 degrees along its transverse or longitudinal axis</cite>.

- **Presentation may be acute or chronic/intermittent, which affects diagnostic difficulty.** <cite id="8b53012a-0">It may present either acutely or with intermittent, recurrent, and chronic symptoms</cite>, and <cite id="8b53012a-3">the presenting symptoms depend on the degree of obstruction, the rapidity of onset, and the type of volvulus</cite>. This variable presentation contributes to missed or delayed diagnosis.

- **Classic acute diagnostic clue: Borchardt triad.** In acute cases, <cite id="27b206b2-0">the Borchardt triad, characterized by pain, retching, and difficulty passing a nasogastric tube, aids diagnosis and is present in up to 70%</cite>. This is one of the most useful bedside clinical patterns.

- **Symptoms range from mild obstruction to necrosis/sepsis, which also signals prognosis.** Patients may have <cite id="2af82b9b-0">mild abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting without emesis</cite>, but severe cases may present with <cite id="2af82b9b-0">sepsis from necrosis of their volvulus</cite>. Thus, signs of ischemia, necrosis, perforation, shock, or sepsis indicate a worse prognosis.

- **The major prognostic determinants are delay, strangulation, and infarction.** <cite id="f2fa1533-6">The reported overall mortality rates range from 30-50%, as a result of delayed recognition and treatment</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="f2fa1533-1">overall mortality is 30%–50% for acute gastric volvulus, increasing to 60% if strangulation or infarction occurs</cite>. Some more recent summaries note improved outcomes with modern care: <cite id="f2fa1533-9">due to advances in diagnosis and management, the mortality from acute gastric volvulus is now 15%-20%, and that for chronic gastric volvulus is 0%-13%</cite>.

In short: the diagnosis of gastric volvulus is most influenced by **clinical pattern (acute vs chronic), Borchardt triad, severity of obstruction, and predisposing anatomy such as paraesophageal/diaphragmatic hernia**, while prognosis is driven mainly by **speed of recognition and whether ischemia, strangulation, infarction, perforation, or sepsis has developed**.

Marfan syndrome type 1 is caused by <cite id="eb3651d7-0">mutations in the gene for fibrillin‐1 (FBN1)</cite>. <cite id="eb3651d7-0">FBN1 was localised to chromosome 15q21.1</cite>, and the disorder is typically autosomal dominant <cite id="eb3651d7-0">with manifestations in multiple organ systems including the skeleton, ocular and cardiovascular systems</cite>.

Its molecular mechanism involves both structural failure of connective tissue and abnormal TGF-β regulation. <cite id="eb3651d7-0">Fibrillin‐1 is the principal component of the 10–12 nm microfibrils found in connective tissue</cite>, and <cite id="eb3651d7-0">in many tissues microfibrils contribute mechanical strength</cite> while <cite id="eb3651d7-0">they also form the scaffold for elastic fibre assembly in elastic tissues</cite>. Beyond structure, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">fibrillin‐1‐rich microfibrils sequester latent complexes of TGFβ and thereby regulate its bioavailability and activation</cite>. As a result, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">MFS and related disorders arise from dysregulation of TGFβ activity</cite>, and <cite id="eb3651d7-0">increased TGFβ signalling has been demonstrated in the lungs, mitral valves and aorta in mouse models of MFS and in the aortic media from patients with MFS</cite>.

At the mutation level, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">mutations in FBN1 include deletions, insertions, missense, nonsense, splice site mutations and in frame changes as well as complete gene deletions</cite>. Mechanistically, these fall into two major classes: <cite id="eb3651d7-0">some mutations produce a shortened transcript degraded by the nonsense mediated decay mechanism, and therefore a reduced amount of fibrillin‐1</cite> (haploinsufficiency), whereas <cite id="eb3651d7-0">others produce altered fibrillin‐1 monomers likely to impair microfibril assembly through a dominant negative mechanism</cite>. In both cases, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">reduced expression of fibrillin‐1 leads to increased TGFβ activation in the lungs, aortic root and mitral valve</cite>, and <cite id="eb3651d7-0">deficient microfibrillar matrix caused by dominant negative mutations in FBN1 similarly results in increased TGFβ activation</cite>.

“Marfan syndrome type 2” refers to a Marfan-like phenotype associated with TGF-β receptor defects. Specifically, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">some patients with classical signs of MFS have been shown to have mutations in TGFBR2 and can be described as having “type 2” MFS</cite>. However, the same review notes that <cite id="eb3651d7-0">another Marfan‐like disorder, now known as Loeys–Dietz syndrome (LDS) ... was shown to result from mutations in the genes for transforming growth factor β receptors 1 and 2 (TGFBR1 and TGFBR2)</cite>, and <cite id="eb3651d7-0">LDS has phenotypic overlap with MFS, but is probably distinct from it</cite>. So “MFS type 2” is best understood as a historical/overlapping label for some TGFBR2-related cases.

For the molecular mechanism in type 2, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">the majority of missense mutations in TGFBR2 identified in MFS2 and LDS involve highly conserved residues in the intracellular serine/threonine kinase domain</cite>, although <cite id="eb3651d7-0">a few nonsense and splice site mutations have also been reported</cite>. Functionally, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">in vitro studies indicate that these mutations impair kinase activity and can act in a dominant negative manner, resulting in the inability of the receptor to propagate signalling after ligand binding and heterodimerisation with TGFBR1</cite>. Paradoxically, despite this predicted signaling loss, <cite id="eb3651d7-0">the increased nuclear localisation of phosphorylated Smad2 and overexpression of TGFβ responsive genes observed in the aortic media in LDS and MFS2 is unexpected</cite>. The proposed explanation is that <cite id="eb3651d7-0">these receptor mutations trigger compensatory upregulation of TGFβ signalling, or alter signalling pathway thresholds with a resultant increase in signalling</cite>.

In short:

- <cite id="eb3651d7-0">MFS1 is due to FBN1 mutations</cite>, causing defective microfibrils, reduced connective-tissue integrity, and excess TGF-β signaling.
- <cite id="eb3651d7-0">MFS2 involves TGFBR2 mutations</cite> in a receptor kinase domain, altering TGF-β receptor function; despite impaired receptor kinase activity, the downstream tissue phenotype is associated with paradoxically increased TGF-β pathway activity in affected tissues.

Timing matters because <cite id="f9ef022e-0">lncRNA levels are being evaluated as early diagnostic biomarkers after ischemic stroke</cite>, and <cite id="d93e2c48-0">sampling time after stroke was a critical factor affecting the accuracy of lncRNA-based diagnosis.</cite>

The clearest available evidence is from a recent systematic review/meta-analysis: <cite id="ed521c63-0">studies that collected samples within 48 hours after stroke showed higher diagnostic sensitivity, 0.81 (95% CI 0.73–0.89).</cite> This implies that <cite id="ed521c63-0">earlier blood collection after onset tends to improve case detection</cite>, while delays can reduce accuracy because the biomarker signal changes over time. That interpretation is consistent with individual-study evidence that <cite id="d93e2c48-7">whole-blood lncRNA expression profiles after ischemic stroke changed significantly with time.</cite>

So, in short: <cite id="d93e2c48-0">the post-onset sampling window materially affects diagnostic performance</cite>, and <cite id="ed521c63-0">collecting samples within the first 48 hours appears to yield better diagnostic sensitivity</cite>. This also means that <cite id="d93e2c48-7">comparing studies or using lncRNAs clinically requires standardized collection times</cite>, because time-dependent expression shifts can otherwise distort diagnostic accuracy.

APOA5 SNPs appear to affect metabolic-syndrome susceptibility mainly by altering triglyceride handling. <cite id="24ad1bf9-5">APOA5 is a key regulator of plasma triglycerides</cite> and <cite id="24ad1bf9-2">APOA5 variation regulates triglyceride and HDL levels</cite>, so variants in this gene can shift several metabolic-syndrome traits at once.

For overall risk, the strongest evidence is for common variants such as rs662799 and rs651821. <cite id="c69cb0bb-0,c69cb0bb-6">A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis found that rs662799 and rs651821 were associated with an approximately 1.5-fold higher likelihood of metabolic syndrome</cite>. <cite id="c69cb0bb-1,d42b3e52-6">Meta-analytic evidence also supports an association of rs3135506 with metabolic syndrome, and specifically indicates that rs662799 increases MetS risk under a dominant model</cite>.

The clearest component affected is hypertriglyceridemia. <cite id="24ad1bf9-0">Cross-sectional studies link rs662799 to high serum triglyceride concentrations</cite>, <cite id="edd6fec0-7">rs651821 has been robustly associated with increased triglyceride concentration and greater vulnerability to hypertriglyceridemia</cite>, and <cite id="edd6fec0-2">APOA5 variants have been associated with the MetS components of higher triglycerides and lower HDL</cite>. HDL effects may be partly secondary to triglyceride changes, because <cite id="c69cb0bb-2,edd6fec0-0">ApoA5 may affect HDL levels through triglyceride metabolism</cite>; additionally, <cite id="edd6fec0-6">rs2075291 could play an important role in triglyceride and HDL-C levels in metabolic syndrome</cite>.

There is also evidence that some APOA5 SNPs worsen insulin resistance and related phenotypes. <cite id="d42b3e52-1">The minor C allele of rs662799 has been reported to produce a worse response in triglyceride levels, insulin levels, and HOMA-IR</cite>, and <cite id="d42b3e52-2">the risk allele of rs662799 was associated with increased HOMA-IR, with a stronger effect in overweight and obese individuals</cite>. Consistently, <cite id="d42b3e52-7">non-C allele carriers of rs662799 showed decreases in triglycerides, insulin, and HOMA-IR after a Mediterranean-profile low-calorie diet</cite>, implying that the risk allele may blunt metabolic improvement.

Evidence for other MetS components is suggestive but less uniform. <cite id="24ad1bf9-9">Triglyceride-raising APOA5 variants may influence susceptibility to obesity</cite>, and <cite id="c69cb0bb-5">APOA5 polymorphisms/haplotypes have been reported to strongly influence systolic and diastolic blood pressure as well as triglycerides</cite>. <cite id="24ad1bf9-1">Because APOA5 regulates triglycerides, that effect may contribute to its observed association with hypertension</cite>.

So, in practical terms, APOA5 SNPs—especially rs662799, rs651821, and rs3135506—seem to increase susceptibility to metabolic syndrome chiefly through <cite id="24ad1bf9-5,24ad1bf9-0,edd6fec0-7">raising triglycerides</cite>, with downstream links to <cite id="edd6fec0-2,c69cb0bb-2">lower HDL</cite> and, in some populations, <cite id="d42b3e52-1,d42b3e52-2">greater insulin resistance</cite>, <cite id="24ad1bf9-9">obesity risk</cite>, and <cite id="c69cb0bb-5,24ad1bf9-1">higher blood pressure/hypertension</cite>.

After a stressor raises adrenal glucocorticoids, <cite id="955b2492-2,b71425c7-1">the HPA axis is shut down by a closed-loop glucocorticoid-dependent negative-feedback system that is essential for terminating the stress response</cite>. <cite id="1e7ad658-3,1e7ad658-7">These glucocorticoids act through glucocorticoid receptors at multiple levels of the axis, including the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus, the anterior pituitary, and hippocampal/forebrain feedback circuits</cite>. 

<cite id="5723501c-1,1e7ad658-0,1e7ad658-1">Activated GRs reduce HPA drive by diminishing excitatory stress input from brainstem pathways and by promoting trans-synaptic inhibition of PVN CRH neurons via forebrain regions such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex</cite>. <cite id="1e7ad658-6,5723501c-8,5723501c-2">At the endocrine level, rising cortisol/glucocorticoids inhibit PVN CRH output and pituitary ACTH release, thereby reducing further adrenal stimulation</cite>. 

<cite id="955b2492-0,e583682b-0,e583682b-4">Feedback can also be rapid: in the PVN, glucocorticoids can quickly suppress CRH-neuron activity through non-genomic mechanisms involving endocannabinoid signaling</cite>. <cite id="b71425c7-1,5723501c-8">Together, these fast and slower GR-mediated actions curb continued glucocorticoid secretion and restore homeostasis after stress</cite>.

<cite id="99b0731d-7">Laparoscopic repair is typically done by first opening the vesicovaginal space at the cervicovaginal junction and dissecting the bladder off the lower anterior uterine wall</cite>, then <cite id="401d742b-3,401d742b-4,401d742b-0">opening the niche and excising/resecting the fibrotic scar tissue and edges of the defect, often back to healthy myometrium</cite>. After excision, <cite id="65e393ac-1,99b0731d-0">the myometrium is re-approximated under direct laparoscopic visualization, most commonly with a two-layer closure designed to avoid entering the uterine cavity</cite>. <cite id="99b0731d-1,99b0731d-2,dc5e0d7f-5,401d742b-1,401d742b-2">Reported closure methods include locking or nonlocking sutures, either running or layered repair; examples include continuous nonlocking 3-0 V-Loc, two-layer absorbable barbed closure, or a first running full-thickness vertical layer followed by a second reinforcing layer with 2-0 Ethibond.</cite>

In acute PID/salpingitis, Doppler ultrasound generally shows an <cite id="e7cabbfb-2">decreased vascular resistance in acute infection</cite>. In a controlled study of acute PID, <cite id="785fd197-0">vascular grading was significantly higher in the study group than the control group</cite>, while <cite id="785fd197-0">the pulsatility index (PI), resistance index (RI), and vascular index (VI) were significantly lower in the study group than control group</cite>. This pattern is consistent with inflammatory hyperemia and low-impedance flow. The same study reported that <cite id="785fd197-0">peak systolic velocity (PS), end diastolic velocity (ED), [and] time average maximum velocity (TAMV)</cite> were measured, but the summary emphasizes the main between-group differences as lower resistance/impedance indices and greater vascularity rather than a single robust velocity marker.

Their clinical usefulness is limited because the evidence base is narrow and mainly supports adjunctive, not stand-alone, diagnosis: <cite id="74d9c60a-0">this review aims to sum up current knowledge on the sensitivity and specificity of ultrasound features suggestive of acute pelvic inflammatory disease</cite>, indicating that diagnostic performance remains an open question rather than a settled standard. Also, Doppler findings do not reliably separate disease subtypes or severity: <cite id="785fd197-0">no significant associations were observed between seven sonographic parameters and acute simple or/and complex cervicitis</cite>. So, although low RI/PI and increased vascularity are more common in acute PID/salpingitis than in controls, Doppler measurements are limited by overlap with other inflammatory pelvic conditions, incomplete validation, and poor discrimination of clinical subgroups.

Laparoscopic excision of a myometrial adenomyoma is typically done by <cite id="S2">making a serosal incision over the myometrial lesion and then excising the adenomyoma</cite>. In some described techniques, <cite id="S5">the uterine serosa and adenomyosis lesion are incised transversely</cite>, and <cite id="S5">vasopressin is injected into the lesion and its margin to reduce local blood flow</cite>. The lesion is then <cite id="S3">sharply dissected from the normal myometrium with a monopolar hook and tenaculum</cite> or <cite id="S1">with a monopolar hook after the plane between adenomyoma and normal tissue is identified</cite>. Surgeons aim to <cite id="S5">resect the lesion as deeply as possible while preserving the serosal layer and avoiding penetration into the uterine cavity</cite>. After removal, <cite id="S2">the uterine defect is closed in one or two layers using a barbed suture</cite>; other reports describe <cite id="S1">single-layer interrupted closure with 2-0 vicryl</cite>.

Key factors for success include:

1. <cite id="S1">Accurate identification of the plane between the adenomyoma and normal myometrium</cite>, which may be aided by <cite id="S3">tactile and finger pressure through the posterior vaginal fornix opening and intracorporeal bimanual palpation</cite>.
2. <cite id="S3">Adequate resection of the adenomyotic tissue</cite>, because <cite id="S3">adenomyosis can be difficult to identify under laparoscopy and treatment may be inappropriate if resection is inadequate</cite>.
3. <cite id="S5">Hemostasis and blood-loss control, such as vasopressin injection</cite>.
4. <cite id="S4">Meticulous repair of the uterine defect</cite>, since <cite id="S4">appropriate repair is one of the most critical steps</cite> and <cite id="S4">closure should avoid dead space, with a flap that is soft and tension free</cite>.
5. <cite id="S5">Preservation of uterine integrity by avoiding entry into the uterine cavity and preserving the serosal layer</cite>.

So, in brief: the procedure involves targeted laparoscopic incision, careful identification and sharp excision of the adenomyoma, blood-loss control, and strong layered uterine reconstruction; success depends mainly on <cite id="S1">finding the correct dissection plane</cite>, <cite id="S3">completely but selectively removing the lesion</cite>, and <cite id="S4">performing secure defect closure without tension or dead space</cite>.

Historically, fallopian tube length has been measured by a few main approaches:

1. <cite id="S1,S3,S7">Direct anatomic/surgical measurement</cite>  
   This is the oldest and most straightforward method: the tube is measured physically from the uterine/proximal end to the fimbrial/distal end, either <cite id="S1">during laparotomy before surgery</cite> or <cite id="S3">on excised specimens using simple tools such as a divider, ruler, or caliper</cite>. More recent pathology work also compares <cite id="S7">gross measurement of removed tubes with pathology-reported lengths</cite>.  
   - Accuracy: generally the best for “true” external length when the tube is intact and measured directly, but <cite id="S1,S2">length decreases after excision and especially after formalin fixation because of tissue shrinkage</cite>.  
   - Application: used in anatomy studies, surgery, and pathology specimens.

2. <cite id="S2,S8,02762552-9">Hysterosalpingography (HSG)</cite>  
   HSG uses contrast X-ray imaging to outline the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes. It has been used preoperatively to estimate tubal length. One study found that <cite id="S2">preoperative hysterosalpingograms suggested a mean tubal length of 7.2 cm, whereas direct measurement of the same tubes averaged 11 cm</cite>, and another report notes that <cite id="S8">the average discrepancy between HSG and direct measurement was about 1 cm, though individual differences could be larger</cite>.  
   - Accuracy: less reliable than direct measurement because it reflects the contrast-filled lumen rather than the actual outer curved tube, and is affected by projection, technique, and tubal configuration.  
   - Application: mainly a clinical imaging method for infertility workup and tubal patency, not the most precise method for anatomic length.

3. <cite id="S4">Ultrasound-based measurement</cite>  
   A later imaging approach measured tubal length by creating a <cite id="S4">2-dimensional image while keeping the tube close to the probe</cite>.  
   - Accuracy: potentially useful in vivo, but operator dependent and limited by how well the tube can be visualized along its entire course.  
   - Application: noninvasive imaging research or selected gynecologic assessment; less historically established than direct measurement or HSG.

4. <cite id="S5">Histologic/serial-section reconstruction</cite>  
   A classic morphologic method, described for oviducts generally, is to <cite id="S5">prepare serial sections and estimate length from the number of sections</cite>.  
   - Accuracy: can be useful for microscopic reconstruction, but is labor-intensive and indirect; it may introduce error from sectioning and tissue processing.  
   - Application: mainly research and histologic studies rather than routine clinical use.

5. <cite id="S5">Threading or tubing the lumen</cite>  
   Another direct research method is to <cite id="S5">insert a transparent tube and measure the length directly</cite>. By analogy, this reflects luminal course rather than simply external straight-line distance.  
   - Accuracy: can better follow the internal path of a tortuous tube, but depends on successful passage and may distort delicate tissue.  
   - Application: experimental/anatomic studies, not routine patient care.

In summary, <cite id="S1,S3">direct measurement on intact tubes at surgery or specimen examination has historically been the reference approach</cite>, whereas <cite id="S2,S8">HSG provides a clinically convenient but less anatomically exact estimate</cite>. <cite id="S1,S2,S7">Postoperative and fixed-specimen measurements tend to be shorter because removal and fixation cause shrinkage</cite>, and <cite id="S4,S5">ultrasound and histologic reconstruction are more specialized methods with narrower applications</cite>.

Clinical trials have assessed IL-2 in acute leukemia mainly as **post-remission maintenance therapy**, especially in AML, and the conclusions differ by **whether IL-2 was given alone or with histamine dihydrochloride (HDC)** and by **remission stage**.

- **AML in first complete remission (CR1): IL-2 monotherapy**
  - A meta-analysis of randomized trials found that <cite id="17f3c967-0">5 RCTs with 905 randomized patients in first complete remission (CR1)</cite> showed <cite id="17f3c967-0">no statistical difference between IL-2 maintenance therapy or control with respect to overall survival (OS) ... disease-free survival (DFS) ... and adverse events</cite>. The conclusion was that <cite id="17f3c967-0">there is no evidence to support the use of IL-2 monotherapy as maintenance therapy in AML patients in first remission</cite>.
  - This is echoed by the individual-patient meta-analysis summary that <cite id="db36cae6-0">IL-2 alone is not an effective remission maintenance therapy for AML patients in CR1.</cite>

- **AML in complete remission after induction/consolidation: HDC + low-dose IL-2**
  - In the key phase III trial, <cite id="98e0f3af-0">320 AML patients in complete remission (CR) after induction and consolidation chemotherapy</cite> were randomized to HDC/IL-2 versus no treatment. The trial <cite id="98e0f3af-0">demonstrated a significant benefit in LFS in the intent-to-treat population, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.71 ... P=0.008</cite>.
  - Safety/tolerability was generally acceptable: <cite id="98e0f3af-0">treatment emergent adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2</cite>; common toxicities were <cite id="98e0f3af-0">injection site reactions (78.4%), flushing (75.0%), headache (68.9%), pyrexia (49.1%), and fatigue (39.6%)</cite>. More severe toxicity was less common: <cite id="98e0f3af-0">grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 26.5%</cite> and <cite id="98e0f3af-0">serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in 5.3%</cite>.
  - Among patients who actually started treatment, efficacy looked stronger: <cite id="98e0f3af-0">LFS HR 0.55 ... and 3-year LFS rates of 40.2% versus 26.2%</cite>.

- **Differences by remission stage**
  - **CR1 patients benefited most:** in post hoc subgroup analysis, <cite id="98e0f3af-0">3-year LFS was 48.0% with HDC/IL-2 versus 27.0% with SOC ... and 3-year overall survival was 61.4% versus 42.3%</cite>.
  - **Second or later remission (CR2+) showed little/no benefit:** <cite id="98e0f3af-0">In these patients there was no significant difference in LFS and no nominal difference in OS between treatment groups</cite>.
  - Longer follow-up supported this pattern: <cite id="98e0f3af-0">OS rates at 6 years [were] 54.8% versus 39.7% in CR1 patients ... and 20.0% versus 27.3% in CR2+ patients</cite> for HDC/IL-2 versus control.
  - Benefit also appeared age-dependent: <cite id="98e0f3af-0">younger patients (<60 years) ... appeared to benefit, while older patients (>60 years) did not appear to benefit</cite>.

- **Pediatric AML in first remission**
  - Pediatric randomized data suggest IL-2 maintenance is **feasible and safe**, but not clearly practice-changing for survival. One phase III summary reported that <cite id="db36cae6-2">Prolonged IL2 for maintenance therapy after intensive chemotherapy is feasible and safe in pediatric AML patients in their first CR.</cite>
  - Another Children’s Oncology Group trial summary states <cite id="db36cae6-5">We randomized 289 children with AML in first remission after intensive chemotherapy to receive IL-2</cite>, with reported outcomes including <cite id="db36cae6-5">51% in the IL-2 group</cite> and <cite id="db36cae6-5">overall survival was 70%</cite>; however, the snippet does not show a clear superiority signal.

Overall: <cite id="17f3c967-0">IL-2 monotherapy in AML CR1 has not improved survival or DFS</cite>, whereas <cite id="98e0f3af-0">HDC plus low-dose IL-2 showed tolerable toxicity and improved leukemia-free survival, especially in younger adults in first complete remission</cite>. In contrast, <cite id="98e0f3af-0">patients in second or later remission did not show a significant benefit</cite>. Pediatric trials suggest <cite id="db36cae6-2">feasibility and safety in first CR</cite>, but the evidence for clear efficacy is weaker than in the adult HDC/IL-2 CR1 setting.

In critical/life-threatening ITP bleeding, guidelines recommend combined high-dose corticosteroids, high-dose IVIG, platelet transfusions, and thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs); IV anti-D immune globulin is another emergency option, used individually or in combination. For actually raising platelets fast, IVIG is the quickest standard therapy, with platelet increases reported within hours and as early as 24 hours. Corticosteroids act more slowly than IVIG, although responses by about 2 days have been reported. Platelet transfusions are used as a temporary bridge in life-threatening bleeding, but the increment may not last and are often given until IVIG takes effect. Anti-D can raise platelets within 24–48 hours, with reported platelet responses of 50%–92% at 24–72 hours in children. TPO-RAs are now recommended as part of emergency combination therapy, but they typically take several days, so they are adjuncts rather than the fastest rescue treatment.

In inflammatory states, ferritin must be interpreted differently: <cite id="a1357f1f-0,f59decd8-0">if ferritin is 100–300 μg/L, TSAT <20% is used to confirm iron deficiency</cite>. For difficult cases, <cite id="bd735dc6-1,bd735dc6-6">soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) can help distinguish IDA from anaemia of inflammation/chronic disease because sTfR rises in iron deficiency but may remain normal in anaemia of inflammation</cite>, and <cite id="1cbe6a9b-0">the sTfR-ferritin index has been reported as especially efficient in inflammatory bowel disease</cite>. Newer erythropoietic markers also help: <cite id="be704ff1-0">reticulocyte haemoglobin content (CHr/Ret-Hb) was more effective than routinely used parameters in a meta-analysis</cite>, with <cite id="ec71a17e-0">reported cutoffs around 25–29 pg for iron deficiency and about 21 pg for IDA</cite>.

The main limitations are that several of these tests are distorted by inflammation or are not specific on their own. <cite id="1cbe6a9b-9,5f245416-2,5f245416-5">Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may be elevated by inflammation, infection, liver disease, malignancy, or chronic disease</cite>, so <cite id="1cbe6a9b-5">a normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency when coexisting disease is present</cite>. <cite id="7746b6ad-3">Serum iron alone is unreliable because of considerable physiologic and diurnal variation</cite>, and <cite id="f59decd8-2">TSAT can be low in both absolute iron deficiency and functional iron deficiency/anemia of inflammation</cite>. <cite id="bd735dc6-2">sTfR is less distorted by inflammation than ferritin</cite>, but <cite id="bd735dc6-0">inflammation can still reduce its sensitivity for true iron deficiency</cite>. Cocaine sweat-patch results depend a lot on both <cite id="4a8f36ed-0">how long the patch is worn</cite> and <cite id="3f94d35b-1">whether use is a single episode or repeated over several days</cite>.

- **Short wear times can miss use.** In one study, <cite id="4a8f36ed-0">the minimum patch wear needed to detect recent or concurrent cocaine use was “more than 2 h and less than or equal to 1 day.”</cite> Controlled-administration data are consistent with that timing: <cite id="8321b5c6-7">cocaine and ecgonine methyl ester were detectable within 2 h, while benzoylecgonine was not detected until 4–8 h after low doses and slightly sooner after high doses.</cite> So, a patch removed too soon is more likely to be falsely negative, especially if the test relies on metabolite confirmation.

- **Longer wear broadens the detection window.** Because the patch samples sweat continuously, <cite id="3f94d35b-1">wearing it for up to 7 days creates a wider time window for detecting cocaine use</cite>. Controlled studies also found that <cite id="4a8f36ed-3">a single 50 mg cocaine exposure may be detectable for up to seven days</cite>. That means the patch is better for “was cocaine used during this interval?” than for pinpointing the exact day or hour of use.

- **Pattern of use matters.** Low-dose or one-time use may be detected, but less reliably than heavier or repeated use. Evidence shows <cite id="8321b5c6-6">positive sweat results have been reported after as little as 1 mg of cocaine</cite>, yet at low doses <cite id="4a8f36ed-4">more than 75% of patches worn for 15 h during the first day were positive for cocaine at the limit of quantification, but only 22% reached ≥25 ng/patch</cite>. In practice, that means very light or isolated use may produce weaker patch concentrations and be more vulnerable to falling below reporting cutoffs, whereas repeated use during the wear period tends to accumulate and be easier to detect.

- **Accuracy is also affected by what happens after use.** Drug amounts on a patch can change with time: <cite id="4a8f36ed-2">cocaine levels in spiked patches declined over 72 h, and levels at 48 h were 30% lower than at 1 h</cite>. So measured concentration is not a simple readout of dose, and concentration alone should be interpreted cautiously.

- **False positives from contamination are possible but limited by design.** The literature indicates <cite id="8321b5c6-0">the patch is relatively impervious to environmental contamination</cite>. Still, contamination has been studied as a reliability issue: <cite id="8321b5c6-2">work on the PharmChek patch specifically examined reliability and false positives from environmental contamination</cite>. Metabolites help here: because <cite id="8321b5c6-7">benzoylecgonine appears after several hours following actual administration</cite>, finding cocaine plus metabolite is generally stronger evidence of true use than cocaine alone.

**Bottom line:** <cite id="4a8f36ed-0">patches usually need at least several hours—and often closer to a day for dependable detection</cite>; <cite id="3f94d35b-1">wearing them for about a week increases the chance of catching any use during that period</cite>. <cite id="4a8f36ed-4">Single low-level use is more likely to yield borderline or cutoff-sensitive results</cite>, while repeated/heavier use across the wear interval is detected more reliably.

First, <cite id="d1bc060e-1">the diagnosis of CTS is clinical in a patient with characteristic symptoms and physical examination findings</cite>, and <cite id="d1bc060e-9">before performing any diagnostic study, a comprehensive review of the patient's history and clinical course, and a complete physical exam is necessary</cite>. Second, electrodiagnostic testing is used when confirmation or clarification is needed, because <cite id="6f6ba3bf-1">electrodiagnostic studies include nerve conduction studies and electromyography</cite> and <cite id="6f6ba3bf-5">electrodiagnosis is commonly used to assess the presence/severity of neuropathic changes and to preclude alternative diagnoses</cite>; similarly, <cite id="6f6ba3bf-0">the physician may obtain electrodiagnostic tests to differentiate among diagnoses</cite>. Third, imaging—especially ultrasound—acts as an adjunct rather than a standalone replacement in most workups, since <cite id="d1bc060e-2">neuromuscular ultrasound probably adds value to electrodiagnostic studies when diagnosing CTS</cite> and <cite id="7d3388ce-1">electrodiagnostic studies add value to ultrasound in quantifying severity of carpal tunnel syndrome</cite>. Together, this means history and examination establish the clinical suspicion, electrodiagnostic tests confirm and grade nerve dysfunction while ruling out mimics, and imaging supplies structural/anatomic information that strengthens or refines the diagnosis.

For recurrent prostate cancer, PET/CT sensitivity/detection generally <cite id="1f858ad1-7">correlates positively with serum PSA levels</cite>—that is, the scan is less sensitive at very low PSA and becomes more sensitive as PSA rises.

Using PSMA PET/CT, reported detection rates are approximately:
- <cite id="1f858ad1-1">30% when PSA is <0.2 ng/mL</cite>
- <cite id="1f858ad1-1">47% when PSA is 0.2–0.49 ng/mL</cite>
- <cite id="1f858ad1-1">65% at higher intermediate PSA levels</cite>

Another review similarly notes that <cite id="1f858ad1-0">at PSA 0.2–0.5 ng/mL, PSMA-PET/CT detects recurrence in about 45–58% of cases</cite>, and that <cite id="1f858ad1-3">detection rates are over 70% when PSA is higher</cite>. One study also reported <cite id="1f858ad1-7">57.9% detection in patients with PSA <0.5 ng/mL</cite>.

So, in short: sensitivity rises substantially with PSA—roughly from about <cite id="1f858ad1-1">30% at PSA <0.2</cite> to around <cite id="1f858ad1-0">45–58% at PSA 0.2–0.5</cite>, and to <cite id="1f858ad1-3">70%+</cite> once PSA is higher.

The main difficulty in segmenting nuclear medicine images is that <cite id="cf3373ad-5">PET and SPECT are confounded by high noise levels and low spatial resolution</cite>, and in PET this leads to <cite id="9cb68426-5">partial volume effect (PVE) ... due to relatively poor spatial resolution</cite>, a major source of information loss. Segmentation pipelines also have to handle <cite id="cf3373ad-2">3D</cite> data with <cite id="cf3373ad-2">large variations in resolution</cite> that <cite id="cf3373ad-2">contain noise</cite>, as well as learning problems such as <cite id="cf3373ad-3">sample imbalance</cite> and, in PET/SPECT more broadly, <cite id="28734457-9">limited data availability</cite>. Deep learning has helped by making segmentation more effective for downstream quantification—<cite id="2b8b4cdd-0">Using DL to segment medical images can help doctors confirm tumor sizes [and] quantitatively evaluate treatment effects</cite>—and by exploiting hybrid imaging: <cite id="7a110ea0-5">dynamic multi-modal fusion</cite> can <cite id="7a110ea0-5">effectively exploit the metabolic and anatomical information from PET and CT</cite>. It has also improved data efficiency and image quality through approaches such as <cite id="4850f364-0">a few-shot u-net deep learning model for lung cancer lesion segmentation via pet/ct imaging</cite> and image-enhancement models, since <cite id="4850f364-1">Supervised deep-learning models have shown great potential in reducing radiotracer dose and scan times without sacrificing image quality</cite>.

Effective management of metastatic melanoma brain metastases is usually <cite id="d84264e9-0,d84264e9-3">a multidisciplinary combination of systemic therapy and local therapy</cite>. For <cite id="069f1f4a-0,069f1f4a-8">asymptomatic melanoma brain metastases, nivolumab plus ipilimumab is a key first-line systemic option, with a 55% intracranial response rate and durable clinical benefit</cite>. In <cite id="e02623e5-2,e02623e5-6">BRAF V600–mutant disease, dabrafenib plus trametinib is another important systemic option because it produced about a 58% intracranial response rate</cite>. However, <cite id="d84264e9-0,d84264e9-1,d84264e9-3">patients with symptomatic brain metastases should receive upfront local therapy—radiosurgery and/or radiation therapy and/or surgery—regardless of the systemic therapy used</cite>, and <cite id="b616b7fb-3,069f1f4a-1">symptomatic melanoma brain metastases have worse outcomes with immunotherapy alone, so localized treatment is usually needed for control</cite>. In practice, <cite id="529cbe12-1,529cbe12-0">stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a standard local treatment with excellent local control; one series reported an 87.1% brain-metastasis local control rate after SRS</cite>. The strongest modern strategy is often <cite id="5ea20f7b-0,529cbe12-5">to combine SRS with immune checkpoint inhibitors, especially concurrently, because this has been associated with improved overall survival, local control, distant brain control, and better 1-year survival/brain control</cite>, with <cite id="529cbe12-3,529cbe12-5">available data suggesting concurrent pembrolizumab/brain RT can be safe and a meta-analysis reporting a 5.3% overall radionecrosis rate</cite>. In short, <cite id="069f1f4a-8,e02623e5-6,d84264e9-3,5ea20f7b-0">systemic therapy controls intracranial and extracranial disease, while surgery/SRS provides rapid local control for symptomatic or threatening lesions, and SRS plus immunotherapy is a commonly favored integrated approach</cite>.

In infectious-disease PET and PET/CT studies, scans are usually read with a <cite id="5c18dc96-0,5660eaa8-0">combination of visual and semiquantitative analysis</cite>. Visually, readers look for <cite id="a22c2b40-3">increased uptake in areas of active infection or inflammation</cite> and distinguish it from <cite id="fdd2541e-2">physiologic FDG uptake</cite>. Semiquantitatively, studies often measure <cite id="5c18dc96-2">SUVmax in the area of suspected infection</cite> and compare it with reference/background activity, with the background <cite id="ec4cf5ff-2">usually measured in muscle, liver, or mediastinal blood pool</cite> and sometimes specifically using <cite id="5c18dc96-2">SUVmean in the blood pool</cite>. Some studies further use <cite id="5660eaa8-5">target-to-background ratios based on liver or aortic blood pool</cite> or a <cite id="fdd2541e-2">five-point scale using liver and mediastinal blood pool SUV measurements</cite> to decide whether uptake is abnormal. In short, abnormal radiotracer uptake is typically defined as focal or disproportionate tracer accumulation in suspected sites that is visually suspicious and/or quantitatively higher than expected physiologic background.

Evidence in head and neck cancer supports PET/CT mainly in three areas:

1. **Tumor volume delineation accuracy**
- PET/CT is widely recognized as useful for RT target definition because it can better depict disease extent and reduce the risk of geographic miss. <cite id="b57c70ec-0">With potentially better identification of the disease extent, i.e., staging, the risk of geographical miss of radiation delivery to the gross tumor volume is reduced.</cite>
- Reviews of HNSCC report that PET/CT can materially alter the defined gross tumor volume and staging. <cite id="1d5cbe12-0">Emerging applications are precise delineation of the tumor volume for radiation treatment planning</cite> and <cite id="d5b78e41-0">PET/CT can change the gross tumor volume (GTV) and staging</cite>.
- Comparative studies show PET-based primary tumor volumes often differ from CT-only contours. <cite id="d5b78e41-1">GTVs of the primary tumor were significantly smaller in 80% of the cases when defined on 18F-FDG-PET/CT as compared to when delineated on CT alone.</cite>
- But the accuracy evidence is mixed rather than absolute: direct comparison with pathology in oral cavity SCC found that standard PET thresholding methods did not reliably reproduce pathologic tumor volume. <cite id="66be48b3-0">Multiple MTV's were associated with pathologic tumor volume; however the correlation was poor (R2 range 0.29–0.58).</cite> <cite id="66be48b3-0">Common SUV thresholds fail to predict pathologic tumor volume in head and neck cancer.</cite> So PET/CT appears helpful as an **adjunct**, but segmentation method matters.

2. **Impact on treatment planning**
- PET/CT improves delineation of both primary tumors and nodal disease and can support biologically guided dose escalation. <cite id="e1ff923a-1">PET/CT improves target delineation for primary tumors and lymph nodes, also allowing for dose escalation in metabolically highly active lesions</cite>.
- It improves nodal detection in HNSCC, which is important because nodal definition directly affects radiation fields. <cite id="e1ff923a-0">Multimodality imaging including 18F-FDG-PET has improved the detection threshold of nodal metastases in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).</cite>
- Published experience indicates PET/CT changes RT target volumes in a meaningful minority of patients. <cite id="8de88476-5">Modification of target volumes in ≤20% of cases with use of PET-CT has been shown in many publications, compared with CT alone.</cite>
- The rationale is not only anatomic but biologic: PET/CT can identify subvolumes such as hypoxic regions for escalation or adaptation. <cite id="b57c70ec-0">PET/CT can identify biological target volumes either for escalation of radiation dose or to predict the requirement for the addition of a radiosensitizer or alternative treatment strategies.</cite>

3. **Prognostic significance**
- PET-derived volumetric biomarkers have prognostic value in HNSCC. A meta-analysis of 15 studies found that higher MTV and TLG predicted worse outcomes. <cite id="bb1d0464-0">The present study included 15 primary studies involving HNSCC cases.</cite> <cite id="bb1d0464-0">For elevated TLG, it attained the pooled HR of 1.85 ... in predicting overall survival (OS), whereas that for elevated MTV was 1.22 ...</cite> <cite id="bb1d0464-0">For elevated MTV, it attained the pooled HR of 1.34 ... in predicting disease-free survival (DFS)</cite>.
- The same meta-analysis concluded that PET/CT has prognostic utility overall. <cite id="bb1d0464-0">This work indicated that PET/CT is of predictive significance across HNSCC cases.</cite>
- During-treatment PET metrics may also stratify risk: <cite id="d5b78e41-7">Higher TLG (>19.0) on FDG PET/CT during RT was a poor prognostic factor for overall survival (OS) (p = 0.001) and progression-free survival (PFS)</cite>.
- Beyond FDG tumor volume, hypoxia PET also has prognostic relevance. <cite id="b57c70ec-0">18F-FMISO has been shown to be both a predictive and prognostic biomarker in head and neck cancer (HNC).</cite> <cite id="b57c70ec-0">Several studies have shown that the level of hypoxia depicted by 18F-FMISO PET before treatment correlates with loco-regional failure</cite>.

**Bottom line:** PET/CT in head and neck cancer is supported as an important **adjunct** for target delineation, especially for nodal disease and biologically guided RT planning, and PET-derived volumetric parameters such as MTV/TLG carry prognostic information. However, evidence also shows that **standard PET segmentation thresholds do not always match pathologic tumor volume**, so PET/CT should complement rather than replace high-quality anatomic imaging and expert contouring.

At the cellular level, <cite id="d8730d8f-0">bone remodeling is carried out by osteoclasts and osteoblasts and is orchestrated by osteocytes</cite>. <cite id="d8730d8f-4,60bf3c8a-9">Thyroid hormones regulate multiple bone cell types, acting mainly via TRα in osteoblasts</cite>; in these cells, <cite id="60bf3c8a-2,d8730d8f-7">T3 promotes osteoblast differentiation and activity through pathways such as IGF-1 and BMP signaling</cite>. Thyroid hormone also <cite id="f0d7edf2-3">stimulates osteoclast differentiation</cite>, so its net effect is to increase bone turnover by accelerating both formation and resorption.  

The pituitary gland regulates this system largely through TSH. <cite id="60bf3c8a-3">TSH has direct effects on both osteoblastic bone formation and osteoclastic bone resorption</cite>, and these actions are <cite id="6e2b20fe-4">linked to TSH receptors expressed in bone cells</cite>. On the resorption side, <cite id="f0d7edf2-1">TSH inhibits osteoclast formation and survival by attenuating JNK/c-jun and NFκB signaling triggered by RANK-L and TNFα</cite>. On the formation side, <cite id="60bf3c8a-0,60bf3c8a-6">TSH stimulates osteoblast differentiation and function and overall exerts anabolic, osteoprotective effects on bone</cite>. So, in simple terms, <cite id="d8730d8f-4,60bf3c8a-2,f0d7edf2-1,60bf3c8a-6">thyroid hormones tend to drive bone-cell activity and turnover, while pituitary TSH provides a direct restraining and protective signal—especially by suppressing osteoclastogenesis and supporting osteoblast maturation</cite>.

<cite id="c15d9a6f-0,c15d9a6f-3">Metyrapone and osilodrostat inhibit 11β-hydroxylase/CYP11B1, the final step in cortisol synthesis, which causes accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol.</cite> <cite id="c15d9a6f-2,3bf00d90-2">That precursor can cross-react in many cortisol immunoassays, producing falsely high cortisol results.</cite> This matters clinically because <cite id="3bf00d90-0,3bf00d90-5">overestimation of cortisol can lead to erroneous dose titration decisions</cite> and <cite id="3bf00d90-1,3bf00d90-4">can cause over-treatment, missed hypoadrenalism, and even potentially fatal hypocortisolaemic/adrenal crisis.</cite> Therefore, <cite id="7c29688f-3,c15d9a6f-7">cortisol should be monitored with interference-free assays—typically LC-MS/MS or assays validated not to cross-react with 11-deoxycortisol—during treatment with adrenal steroid synthesis inhibitors.</cite>

<cite id="fcc312f5-0">The systematic review found that oral complications studied with positioning stents included xerostomia, salivary changes, dysphagia, and pain on swallowing.</cite> For xerostomia specifically, <cite id="d4c35217-4">it can be assessed objectively by salivary flow rate measurement or subjectively by questionnaire,</cite> and <cite id="d4c35217-0">overall, the reported risk of xerostomia decreased when positioning stents were used, in both objective and subjective assessments.</cite>

However, the evidence is not strong enough to conclude a definite benefit: <cite id="fcc312f5-0">the review concluded that there is insufficient evidence that positioning stents have a preventive effect against xerostomia</cite> and called for <cite id="fcc312f5-0">more high-quality prospective trials with long-term follow-up.</cite>

So, in brief: positioning stents appear to be associated with <cite id="d4c35217-0">lower measured salivary dysfunction/dry mouth and better patient-reported xerostomia symptoms</cite>, but <cite id="fcc312f5-0">the current evidence after head and neck radiotherapy/chemoradiotherapy remains limited and inconclusive.</cite>

Radiation-induced senescent epithelial and endothelial cells damage lung tissue mainly by creating a <cite id="f72c9381-0">pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)</cite> that persists in injured tissue and drives pathology rather than repair <cite id="f72c9381-0">when senescent cells persist in damaged tissues, they can contribute to tissue degeneration and inflammatory diseases</cite>.

For epithelial cells, especially alveolar type 2 cells, the key mechanism is paracrine signaling through SASP factors. <cite id="808472dc-1">Senescent AT2 cell clearance reduces the expression of SASP factors such as IL-6, TGF-β, and MMP12</cite>, implying that these molecules are major effectors of injury. These signals promote fibrotic remodeling because <cite id="808472dc-3">alveolar epithelial cell senescence, cell cycle arrest, and the SASP may contribute to the development and perpetuation of fibrotic scarring</cite>. In addition, epithelial SASP can act on stromal cells: <cite id="808472dc-7">senescent cells secrete increased amounts of IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-8, which can induce the differentiation of fibroblasts into</cite> profibrotic myofibroblast-like cells, thereby amplifying extracellular matrix deposition and fibrosis.

A particularly important epithelial-to-endothelial signal is CCL2. <cite id="1dd0e9db-8">Radiation-induced epithelial senescence leads to increased SASP factor production, in particular Ccl2, by senescent bronchial-alveolar epithelial cells</cite>. That CCL2 is pathogenic is supported by the observation that <cite id="1dd0e9db-0">RT-induced vascular dysfunction and associated adverse effects can be efficiently antagonized by inhibition of Ccl2 signaling</cite> and that <cite id="1dd0e9db-1">the SASP-factor Ccl2 fosters vascular dysfunction and endothelial cell loss in radiation-induced lung disease</cite>. So, senescent epithelial cells injure the lung not only by promoting fibrosis, but also by damaging the pulmonary microvasculature through CCL2-mediated paracrine signaling.

For endothelial cells, radiation-induced senescence contributes directly to vascular pathology. <cite id="1dd0e9db-3">An accumulation of senescent endothelial cells around radiation-induced lung focal lesions</cite> has been observed, and endothelial senescence itself causes dysfunction because <cite id="1dd0e9db-7">endothelial cell senescence can lead to endothelial dysfunction by dysregulation of vasodilation and hemostasis</cite>. This means senescent endothelial cells impair vascular homeostasis, promoting abnormal permeability, thromboregulatory imbalance, and microvascular loss, which worsens tissue hypoxia, inflammation, and remodeling.

In short: radiation drives epithelial and endothelial cells into senescence; these cells then secrete SASP mediators such as <cite id="808472dc-1">IL-6, TGF-β, and MMP12</cite> and <cite id="1dd0e9db-8">CCL2</cite>, which act in autocrine and paracrine ways to sustain inflammation, activate fibroblasts, induce fibrotic scarring, and cause endothelial dysfunction and cell loss. <cite id="808472dc-3">This promotes fibrotic scarring</cite> while <cite id="1dd0e9db-1">fostering vascular dysfunction and endothelial cell loss</cite>, together producing progressive lung tissue damage.

Based on findings across multiple studies in NAFLD, better adherence to a Mediterranean Diet appears to improve anthropometric measures, but the strength of evidence differs by outcome.

- **BMI:** The clearest consistent benefit is for BMI. A 2020 systematic review/meta-analysis of 6 trials and 7 observational studies found that the Mediterranean Diet <cite id="aff34e81-0">“showed a significant decreasing effect on BMI (ES = -1.23 kg/m²; 95% CI: -2.38, -0.09)”</cite>.
- **Waist circumference:** In that same meta-analysis, the effect on waist circumference was not statistically significant; <cite id="aff34e81-0">“no significant effect was observed in waist circumference”</cite>.
- **Body weight and waist circumference in individual prospective data:** Not all studies are null for these outcomes. In the FLIPAN prospective trial, NAFLD patients with higher Mediterranean Diet adherence <cite id="836a7b1e-0">“showed higher decreases in BMI, body weight, WC”</cite>, suggesting that stronger adherence may help reduce all three measures in practice.
- **Body weight from broader pooled evidence:** More recent pooled evidence also suggests weight loss is possible with Mediterranean Diet interventions; one meta-analytic summary reported the diet <cite id="662f24f7-0">“significantly reduced body weight [weighted mean difference (WMD = −2.38 kg”</cite>.

Overall: <cite id="aff34e81-0">BMI reduction is the most consistently supported anthropometric benefit</cite>; <cite id="836a7b1e-0">body weight and waist circumference may also decrease when adherence is high</cite>, but <cite id="aff34e81-0">evidence for waist circumference is less consistent across pooled studies</cite>.

<cite id="2f09e39d-0">This 2023 meta-analysis included 12 randomized trials (794 patients) with NAFLD.</cite> Overall, <cite id="2f09e39d-0">vitamin E supplementation reduced ALT by about 7–10 IU/L</cite> and <cite id="2f09e39d-0">reduced AST by about 4.7–5.6 IU/L</cite>, showing that the effect on ALT was generally larger than on AST.

For the adult vs pediatric comparison, the available evidence indicates that <cite id="9866a02d-1">vitamin E decreased blood levels of liver enzymes in adults</cite> and <cite id="9866a02d-2">vitamin E supplementation consistently reduced serum levels of ALT and AST in both pediatric and adult subjects.</cite> However, pediatric findings appear less consistent in some trials: <cite id="9866a02d-5">vitamin E or metformin does not result in sustained reduction of ALT levels in children and adolescents.</cite>

So, in practical terms: <cite id="2f09e39d-0,9866a02d-1">adults tend to show clearer and more consistent reductions in both ALT and AST, with ALT falling more than AST.</cite> In <cite id="9866a02d-2,9866a02d-5">children and adolescents, vitamin E can also lower ALT and AST, but the improvement—especially for sustained ALT reduction—has been more variable across studies.</cite>

<cite id="bf2bfc9d-2">The studies reviewed showed reduced mean vitamin B-12 status and elevated mean homocysteine concentrations in vegetarians, particularly among vegans.</cite> This happens largely because <cite id="bf2bfc9d-5">vegetarians are known to be deficient in vitamin B12, due to a lack of dietary animal products</cite>, and <cite id="8b112a24-0">vitamin B12, in the form of methylcobalamin, is an essential co-factor for methionine synthase and the remethylation of homocysteine</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="8b112a24-3">Me-Cbl functions as a cofactor for methionine synthase and converts homocysteine to methionine with the help of vitamin B6 and folate</cite>. So when B12 is deficient, homocysteine is not efficiently remethylated to methionine, causing it to accumulate.

The health relevance is that <cite id="bf2bfc9d-7">homocysteine is associated with a 20% increased risk of circulatory health problems</cite>, and there is also evidence that <cite id="bf2bfc9d-1">subclinical B12 deficiency increases the risk of cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease (especially stroke), early mortality</cite>. In vegetarians specifically, <cite id="bf2bfc9d-3">not taking vitamin B12 supplements or regularly eating B12-fortified foods may explain the higher stroke risk found among vegetarians</cite>.

In short: vegetarian diets—especially vegan diets—can provide too little B12 unless fortified foods or supplements are used; B12 deficiency impairs the methionine synthase reaction that normally clears homocysteine; the resulting hyperhomocysteinemia is linked to vascular and neurologic risk, including circulatory disease, stroke, and cognitive decline.

The clinical-trial literature on pistachios and glycaemic control has a fairly consistent profile:

- <cite id="661b85d3-0">It is based on randomised controlled trials</cite>, and <cite id="661b85d3-0">the 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis included eight RCTs</cite>.
- The studied populations were <cite id="661b85d3-0">individuals with a high risk of CVD</cite>, with relatively few trials in established diabetes; the review noted <cite id="661b85d3-0">limited availability of studies with diabetic cases and relatively small sample sizes</cite>.
- Many trials focused on dysglycaemia/prediabetes. For example, <cite id="3306342f-0">a 12-week trial in Asian Indians with prediabetes used a premeal load of 60 g pistachios</cite>, and another review snippet indicates <cite id="df1100d4-1">57 g/d pistachios for 4 months improved fasting plasma glucose and fasting plasma insulin in adults with prediabetes</cite>.
- Trial designs have included both chronic feeding studies and acute postprandial studies. One cited study was <cite id="3306342f-1">a randomized, controlled, crossover trial</cite>, while another was an <cite id="3306342f-2">acute-effect study showing improved postprandial glucose, insulin, and GLP-1 responses</cite>.
- Interventions generally tested pistachios <cite id="661b85d3-0">exchanged isocalorically for other foods</cite>, rather than simply added on top of habitual intake.
- The main glycaemic outcomes assessed were <cite id="661b85d3-0">fasting blood sugar (FBS), fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR</cite>; some newer trials also reported <cite id="3306342f-0">HbA1c</cite> and acute postprandial responses <cite id="3306342f-2">such as glucose, insulin, and GLP-1</cite>.
- Overall, the body of RCT evidence suggests modest benefit: the meta-analysis found that pistachio consumption <cite id="661b85d3-0">decreased FBS by 5.32 mg/dl and insulin by 1.86 µIU/ml</cite>, although <cite id="661b85d3-0">no significant change was observed for HOMA-IR overall</cite>. In subgroup findings, <cite id="df1100d4-0">glycaemic control improved in T2DM patients by reducing FBS and HOMA-IR</cite>.

In short: the key trials have mostly been <cite id="661b85d3-0">small randomized interventions in people with prediabetes or other cardiometabolic risk</cite>, often using about <cite id="df1100d4-1">57 g/day</cite> or <cite id="3306342f-0">60 g/day</cite> of pistachios for <cite id="3306342f-0">12 weeks</cite> to <cite id="df1100d4-1">4 months</cite>, with outcomes centered on fasting glucose/insulin and, in some studies, HbA1c or postprandial glycaemia.

Randomized controlled trials suggest that Licorice Flavonoid Oil (LFO) has <cite id="39e0f745-0">modest but statistically significant anti-obesity effects in overweight adults</cite>, with evidence of a <cite id="39e0f745-0">dose-dependent body fat–reducing effect</cite>.

- In the earlier dose-finding RCT, <cite id="f34e3986-0">an 8-week clinical trial showed that GLFO (300–900 mg/kg) decreased the visceral fat area, body weight, BMI, and LDL-cholesterol levels, and no adverse ...</cite> The highest clearly reported effective dose in the abstracted literature was <cite id="f34e3986-9">LFO (900 mg/day) resulted in significant decreases from baseline levels in visceral fat area, body weight, BMI, and LDL-cholesterol.</cite> This indicates that higher doses were associated with measurable reductions not only in weight-related metrics but also in cardiometabolic risk markers.

- In the longer-term placebo-controlled trial, <cite id="39e0f745-0">a placebo-controlled, double-blind, long-term (12 weeks) ingestion study at 300 mg/day, the minimal effective dose observed in the dose finding study</cite> enrolled overweight adults, and <cite id="39e0f745-0">body weight increased in the placebo group, but was maintained at close to pre-ingestion level in the LFO group, resulting in significant (p < 0.05) differences in the changes in body weight and BMI between the LFO group and the placebo group at each time-point.</cite> The same trial reported that <cite id="39e0f745-0">the weight-reducing effect was attributable to...</cite> body-fat reduction, and the paper states that <cite id="dad26a34-7">LFO suppressed body weight gain by reducing body fat mass in overweight subjects.</cite>

Clinical significance:
- The effect appears to be <cite id="39e0f745-0">more preventive/moderating than dramatic</cite> at 300 mg/day: participants largely avoided the weight gain seen in placebo rather than showing large absolute weight loss. That makes the 300 mg/day dose clinically relevant mainly for <cite id="39e0f745-0">weight maintenance and limiting fat accumulation in overweight individuals</cite>.
- The 900 mg/day data appear more clinically meaningful for active weight reduction because <cite id="f34e3986-9">significant decreases from baseline levels in visceral fat area, body weight, BMI, and LDL-cholesterol</cite> suggest benefit beyond the scale, especially given the importance of visceral fat and LDL as cardiometabolic risk factors.
- Overall, the trials indicate that <cite id="39e0f745-0">300 mg/day was identified as the minimal effective dose</cite>, while <cite id="f34e3986-9">900 mg/day</cite> produced clearer reductions in adiposity-related outcomes. However, based on the available snippets, the magnitude of weight loss seems <cite id="39e0f745-0">modest</cite>, so LFO should be viewed as a possible adjunct rather than a stand-alone obesity treatment.

In one sentence: <cite id="39e0f745-0">300 mg/day helped prevent weight gain and reduce body fat over 12 weeks</cite>, whereas <cite id="f34e3986-9">900 mg/day produced significant reductions in visceral fat, body weight, BMI, and LDL-cholesterol over 8 weeks</cite>, making higher-dose LFO more clinically meaningful for cardiometabolic improvement than for large absolute weight loss.

<cite id="6d7b14e0-0">Three RCTs found no relationship between self-weighing and mood state.</cite> In particular, <cite id="6d7b14e0-0">one study randomized 30 overweight adults to daily weighing or weekly weighing</cite>, and the trial evidence indicates <cite id="95c1515a-0">a weight-loss intervention that focuses on daily self-weighing does not cause adverse psychological outcomes.</cite>

So, for overweight adults, randomized controlled trials suggest that increasing self-weighing frequency from weekly to daily <cite id="6d7b14e0-0">does not worsen mood state</cite> and <cite id="95c1515a-0">does not produce adverse psychological outcomes</cite>, implying no clear increase in depression symptoms either within these trials.

Computed tomographic colonography (CTC, or “virtual colonoscopy”) offers several practical advantages for colorectal cancer screening: <cite id="6efc6eff-8">it is less invasive and does not involve anesthesia</cite>, <cite id="6efc6eff-3">it is quick (about 10–20 minutes)</cite>, and <cite id="97eeb286-2">it has a much lower risk of colon perforation than conventional colonoscopy</cite>. In performance terms, <cite id="97eeb286-3">CT colonography is as sensitive as colonoscopy for large adenomas and colorectal cancer</cite>, and <cite id="6efc6eff-0">when used alone it can be done every 5 years</cite>. Timing and patient selection appear to be the two main determinants of whether thrombolysis for acute CRAO has a plausible benefit-risk profile.

For IV alteplase specifically, the stroke-style window most often used is **within 4.5 hours**: <cite id="572514ab-1">34 patients received IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of symptom onset and 50% (17 out of 34) had recovery of functional visual acuity</cite>, and <cite id="572514ab-8">IVT within 4.5 hours after symptom onset may represent an effective treatment of NA-CRAO</cite>. By contrast, more recent randomized evidence is less encouraging, as <cite id="a507eefa-4">IV administration of the thrombolytic agent within 4.5 hours of CRAO onset led to vision recovery in eight of 40 patients versus nine of 38</cite>, and another report found <cite id="572514ab-4">only 4 patients in each group achieved functional visual recovery</cite>. Overall, earlier treatment likely improves the chance of retinal salvage, but efficacy remains uncertain.

- **Patient selection:** Thrombolysis is generally discussed for **non-arteritic CRAO**, not arteritic disease. Several sources specify treatment in <cite id="572514ab-8">NA-CRAO</cite> or <cite id="a507eefa-7">non-arteritic CRAO</cite>. Standard thrombolysis exclusions also matter: <cite id="a507eefa-1">Intravenous tPA is used in patients within 4.5 hours of the incident if there is no intracranial or systemic hemorrhage</cite>.

- **Safety:** Safety appears acceptable in carefully selected early presenters, especially for IV alteplase. A recent review reported that <cite id="a507eefa-0">none of the 60 cases that received IV alteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset developed</cite> major symptomatic complications (the review specifically describes reassuring safety). Another ophthalmology summary likewise noted <cite id="572514ab-4">There were no safety concerns noted</cite>. Still, because randomized efficacy data are mixed, a favorable safety profile alone does not establish clear benefit.

**Bottom line:** <cite id="a507eefa-8">Intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) with alteplase in a time window < 4.5 h may lead to a favorable outcome</cite>, but the apparent benefit depends heavily on **ultra-early treatment**, **excluding arteritic or hemorrhagic mimics/contraindications**, and possibly selecting patients with **incomplete/non-arteritic CRAO**.
