Different modifiers affect magnesium-carbonate flotation mainly in three ways: <cite id="99d3775f-0">they regulate pulp pH, alter collector speciation and adsorption, and selectively depress one carbonate relative to another, which changes grade and recovery.</cite>

- **pH control:** <cite id="99d3775f-0">Flotation of Mg carbonates is dependent on solution pH, so modifiers are used as pH regulators.</cite> <cite id="99d3775f-0">Changing pH alters the ionization degree and stability of collector species, solution chemistry, electrostatic properties of minerals/reagents, and the amount/species of precipitates in the pulp.</cite> As a result, flotation response can shift strongly with pH. For example, with sodium oleate, <cite id="99d3775f-0">magnesite and dolomite recoveries significantly increased with increasing sodium oleate concentration under weak acidic to alkaline conditions,</cite> and under one optimum condition <cite id="99d3775f-0">dolomite recovery was around 90% while magnesite recovery was around 72% at pH 10 and 4 × 10−4 mol/L sodium oleate.</cite>

- **Interaction with collectors:** Modifiers influence how collectors adsorb. For anionic collectors, <cite id="99d3775f-0">sodium oleate can adsorb on magnesite and dolomite by chemisorption,</cite> but <cite id="99d3775f-0">pH and species concentration affect collector interactions with the mineral surface.</cite> Mixed collectors can improve this further: <cite id="99d3775f-0">the sodium oleate/dodecylamine mixed collector (3:1) showed higher selectivity than sodium oleate alone under weakly acidic conditions, because heteropolar interaction reduced electrostatic repulsion and increased collector adsorption on dolomite.</cite> Also, <cite id="99d3775f-0">sodium oleate and oleic acid can react with dissolved Mg2+ to form (RCOO)2Mg precipitates, improving collector interaction with dolomite and increasing floatability.</cite>

- **Effect of pH on cationic collectors:** With amine collectors, pH is critical because the active collector species changes. <cite id="99d3775f-0">Dodecylamine chloride can effectively separate dolomite from magnesite over pH 5–9, with dolomite recoveries around 80% and magnesite recoveries around 20%.</cite> The reason is that <cite id="99d3775f-0">protonated amine species is a more effective collector than neutral species for dolomite flotation at pH 5,</cite> and <cite id="99d3775f-0">the collecting power becomes very weak under alkaline conditions because protonated amine concentration diminishes.</cite>

- **Depressants and selective recovery:** Depressants improve separation by suppressing one mineral’s floatability. <cite id="99d3775f-0">They can change electrostatic interaction between collector and mineral and/or make the mineral surface more hydrophilic.</cite> For example:
  - <cite id="99d3775f-0">In dodecylamine chloride flotation, sodium hexametaphosphate significantly decreased dolomite recovery while magnesite recovery changed only slightly, enabling effective separation.</cite>
  - <cite id="99d3775f-0">The mechanism was increased negative zeta potential of dolomite due to adsorption of phosphate species, lowering collector–dolomite affinity.</cite>
  - <cite id="99d3775f-0">Sodium silicate also decreased both dolomite and magnesite recoveries with dodecylamine chloride, but the effect was stronger for dolomite, producing selective separation.</cite>
  - In sodium oleate systems, <cite id="99d3775f-0">sodium hexametaphosphate can depress magnesite more strongly than dolomite.</cite> Under optimum dosage, <cite id="99d3775f-0">sodium hexametaphosphate and CMC gave dolomite grade and recovery of about 94.47% and 87.41%, respectively.</cite>
  - <cite id="99d3775f-0">CMC alone and CMC mixed with sodium metasilicate generated dolomite recoveries of about 73% and 83%, respectively,</cite> because <cite id="99d3775f-0">these mixed depressants adsorbed strongly on magnesite and only slightly on dolomite.</cite>
  - <cite id="99d3775f-0">Soluble starch also selectively depressed magnesite and enabled a dolomite recovery of 92.3%.</cite>

**Overall:** <cite id="99d3775f-0">Modifiers improve magnesium-carbonate flotation selectivity when they are chosen to control pH, optimize collector species/adsorption, and selectively depress the unwanted carbonate.</cite> In practice, <cite id="99d3775f-0">grade and recovery are the key metrics used to evaluate that selectivity.</cite>

In tholeiitic basalts, CO₂ storage by mineral carbonation is controlled mainly by how temperature and pressure change <cite id="c1326df1-2">water–rock reactions, because CO₂ sequestration in basaltic rocks is stored mainly through mineral carbonation</cite> and by how much dissolved CO₂ is available to react with Ca-, Mg-, and Fe-bearing basaltic minerals. <cite id="b489db12-3">Carbon mineralization occurs when CO₂ is dissolved in water and reacts with Ca-rich minerals from basalts to form stable carbonate minerals.</cite>

**Pressure:** Higher pressure generally improves storage efficiency because it helps keep more CO₂ in a dense phase and supports dissolution into formation water. For geologic storage, <cite id="c1326df1-9">pure CO₂ is typically stored at depths greater than 800 m, where the ambient temperature and pressure exceed the critical point of CO₂ (31°C and 7.3–7.4 MPa)</cite>. In practice, that means deeper basalt reservoirs can hold more CO₂ per unit volume and maintain stronger fluid–rock contact, which favors carbonation. Pressure is also recognized as one of the variables controlling how fast and how extensively carbonation proceeds: <cite id="b489db12-8">the degree to which mineral carbonation is significant in a storage reservoir and at what rate mineralization occurs depends on rock type, pressure and ...</cite>

**Temperature:** Temperature has a mixed effect. On one hand, warmer conditions can accelerate basalt dissolution and reaction kinetics, helping release reactive cations for carbonate formation. On the other hand, very high temperature can reduce CO₂ solubility in water, leaving less dissolved CO₂ available for reaction. The literature therefore points to an optimum rather than “the hotter the better.” For basaltic storage, <cite id="c1326df1-7">mineral storage of CO₂ could theoretically be executed at depths greater than 1500 m in basaltic rocks outside of the geothermal ...</cite> and modeling work highlights <cite id="91cd9d98-2">mineral carbonation in basalts at low temperature (20–50°C)</cite>, showing that effective mineral trapping does not require extreme heat. Consistent with that, experimental work reports <cite id="c1326df1-5">significant carbonation up to 71% for calcium can still be achieved with ... low temperatures</cite>.

**For tholeiitic basalts specifically:** Their composition tends to make them comparatively favorable for carbonation. A recent comparison found that <cite id="b489db12-1">at a given pressure and temperature, picritic basalt and tholeiite exhibit higher ...</cite> carbonation evidence than some other basaltic lithologies. So, under the same P–T conditions, tholeiitic basalt can be relatively efficient because it contains abundant reactive silicate phases.

**Bottom line:**  
- **Increasing pressure** usually improves CO₂ storage efficiency by increasing CO₂ density and supporting dissolved-CO₂ availability for mineral trapping.  
- **Temperature** has a **tradeoff**: moderate temperatures often help kinetics, but too much heat can lower CO₂ solubility; effective basalt carbonation is commonly discussed even at <cite id="91cd9d98-2">20–50°C</cite>.  
- In **tholeiitic basalts**, these effects combine with favorable mineralogy, so at suitable depth and moderate hydrothermal conditions they can mineralize CO₂ rapidly and store it permanently. <cite id="c1326df1-0">The reactive minerals found in basalt facilitate rapid and effective mineral carbonation, enabling efficient storage of CO₂.</cite>

In basalt weathering systems, trace-element reactivity is highly variable rather than uniform: <cite id="d8b3c7af-1">water–rock interaction, pH, and redox control mobility of elements in groundwater</cite>. Under acidic conditions, many transition metals are more reactive and mobile, because <cite id="da411517-6">basalt leaching by weakly acidic, CO2-charged water is the overwhelming source of metals</cite> and <cite id="da411517-2">Ni, Cr, Cu and Zn have greater mobility at low pH conditions</cite>. Redox-sensitive elements behave differently: <cite id="d8b3c7af-2">the geochemical behaviour of Mn, Cr, V, Fe and Ce is very dependent on redox conditions</cite>, and in basaltic groundwater <cite id="da411517-1">V had decreased mobility, and Fe and Mn had increased mobility in anoxic groundwater</cite>. Rare earth elements tend to be remobilized in acidic weathering zones but immobilized where pH rises, since <cite id="d8b3c7af-3">the precipitation of the REE3+ in the rinds and centers of the corestones are likely due to increases of the pH of the weathering solution</cite> and <cite id="d8b3c7af-5">vertical pH and redox gradients in weathering crusts facilitate dissolution of REE-bearing minerals at shallow level and fixation of REE at depth</cite>. Some elements are exceptionally mobile in basaltic environments: <cite id="d8b3c7af-9">the most mobile elements were As and B in all experiments</cite>, and <cite id="d8b3c7af-9">although As concentration in basalts is low, it is highly mobile in shallow basaltic groundwater</cite>. Finally, chemical form matters as much as abundance: <cite id="0d6e56f5-4">arsenic, chromium, and vanadium can form negatively charged ions with oxygen known as oxyanions</cite>, whereas <cite id="0d6e56f5-4">uranium complexes with bicarbonate</cite>, so different basalt-derived trace elements respond very differently to the same environmental conditions.

Deep-ocean conditions make calcium carbonate less stable. <cite id="62c35d70-3">The solubility of calcium carbonate increases with depth, pressure, and lower temperatures, leading to higher dissolution rates in deep waters</cite>. In the deep ocean, calcium carbonate becomes progressively unstable across the lysocline, <cite id="62c35d70-4">the transition zone within which calcium carbonate increasingly becomes chemically unstable and begins to dissolve</cite>, and by about <cite id="62c35d70-0">4000–5000 m there is the “Carbonate Compensation Depth” (CCD) at which calcium carbonate (calcite and aragonite) supply equals the rate of dissolution</cite>. Dissolution is further enhanced when deep/bottom waters are more CO2-rich and corrosive: <cite id="62c35d70-2">the spreading of corrosive (CO2-enriched) bottom waters enhances the dissolution of CaCO3 minerals delivered to the seafloor or contained</cite>.

For serpulid tubes, this means their calcareous skeletons are directly vulnerable because <cite id="8e00ed68-1">Serpulid tubes lack an external organic cover and are in direct contact with seawater that can dissolve structures made of calcium carbonate</cite>. Under deep, cold, corrosive conditions, <cite id="8e00ed68-8">The cold and corrosive waters of the deep ocean (hadal zone) have been observed to partially dissolve the serpulid tubes</cite>. Structurally, serpulid tubes can vary from simple to layered designs: <cite id="8e00ed68-6">Although the walls of most serpulid tubes are homogeneous, tubes of certain species may contain up to four ultrastructurally distinct layers</cite>. Their crystal architecture also matters, since <cite id="8e00ed68-2">Simple and spherulitic prismatic microstructures exhibit the predominantly uniform orientation of calcium carbonate crystals</cite>, and some lineages evolved protection against seawater attack, including <cite id="8e00ed68-1">a dense outer protective tube layer</cite>.

So, in short: increasing pressure, low temperature, and CO2-rich deep waters promote CaCO3 dissolution; in serpulids this can partially dissolve and weaken tubes, favoring protective and sometimes multilayered tube ultrastructures as adaptations to corrosive seawater.

In water treatment, adsorption and biodegradation usually act as a <cite id="8404f351-1">pair of major removal routes for antibiotics in activated sludge</cite>, and for sulfonamides this often means a two-step or overlapping process:

1. <cite id="0a767bbc-0,0a767bbc-3">Sulfonamide molecules first interact with activated sludge through adsorption/sorption</cite> or with added sorbents such as biochar.  
2. Once retained on sludge flocs or sorbent surfaces, <cite id="0a767bbc-0,0a767bbc-8">they can then be biodegraded by microorganisms</cite>, reducing the dissolved concentration in water.

Mechanistically, adsorption works by <cite id="0a767bbc-2">pore filling, surface complexation, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interactions</cite>. This rapid capture step helps by:
- lowering the immediate dissolved sulfonamide concentration,
- bringing the antibiotic into close contact with biomass or biofilms,
- and buffering concentration spikes so microbes have more time to transform the compound.

Biodegradation then converts the adsorbed or dissolved sulfonamides into transformation products and, ideally, more mineralized end products. In many activated-sludge systems, <cite id="0a767bbc-5,8404f351-6">the two sulfonamides studied were predominantly removed by biodegradation</cite>, while adsorption still contributes as an initial partitioning and holding step. Another study similarly found that <cite id="0a767bbc-8">biodegradation is the primary removal mechanism of SDZ and SMZ</cite>.

So the way they work together is:

- <cite id="0a767bbc-0">adsorption temporarily stores sulfonamides on sludge/sorbent surfaces</cite>;
- <cite id="0a767bbc-8">biodegradation destroys part of that stored or dissolved mass</cite>;
- as biodegradation consumes the antibiotic, adsorption sites can effectively be freed, allowing continued uptake.

This combined behavior is often more effective than relying on either process alone: adsorption alone can be reversible, since <cite id="0a767bbc-0">desorption characteristics were important enough to be investigated alongside adsorption and biodegradation</cite>; biodegradation alone can be slower or inhibited at high antibiotic concentrations. Also, sorbent choice matters, because <cite id="0a767bbc-1">conventional biochar has limited effectiveness for sulfonamide adsorption, while modified biochar shows greater adsorption potential</cite>.

In short: <cite id="8404f351-1">adsorption and biodegradation are the main routes</cite>—adsorption captures and concentrates sulfonamides, while biodegradation provides the more permanent removal by transforming them.

Key future priorities are to move from basic natural-history knowledge toward applied ecology, mass rearing, and field validation of control efficacy.

1. **Define habitat requirements well enough for conservation biocontrol.** For *Tetanocera elata*, research should further resolve the habitat features that support natural populations, because <cite id="41dfe102-0">it “has the potential to be developed as a native natural enemy in a conservation biological control programme”</cite> and the habitat study was undertaken <cite id="41dfe102-0">“to better understand the ecological requirements of this species.”</cite> The same study found that <cite id="41dfe102-0">“taller dead vegetation was associated with T. elata presence”</cite>, implying a priority to test how vegetation structure, moisture refuges, and field-edge management can be manipulated to promote the fly in cropping systems.

2. **Develop optimum rearing methods for operational use.** A major applied need is better laboratory/production protocols, because the thesis on *T. elata* states that <cite id="9699efaa-0">the results are discussed “in the context of developing optimum conditions for the rearing of T. elata with the view of using it in biological”</cite> control. That points to priorities such as scalable colony maintenance, reliable oviposition, larval survival, pupariation, and overwintering methods.

3. **Clarify host/prey range and prey-quality effects.** Since <cite id="2cd0bdca-0">“T. elata larval survival outcomes depend on prey slug species”</cite>, future work should identify which pest slugs best support development, which non-target gastropods are attacked, and how prey size/stage and slug community composition affect control performance.

4. **Test compatibility with other slug biocontrol agents.** Integration with nematodes is especially important, because <cite id="2cd0bdca-0">“Successful pupariation in T. elata is reduced for larvae fed on nematode-exposed slugs”</cite> even though <cite id="2cd0bdca-7">“Predatory third instar T. elata larvae appeared to select nematode-exposed D. reticulatum over non-exposed slugs”</cite>. This means future research should determine optimal timing, sequencing, and compatibility of *T. elata* with *Phasmarhabditis hermaphrodita* and other tactics in integrated pest management.

5. **Run realistic field trials to measure pest suppression.** Reviews stress that the field needs stronger nonchemical-control evidence and better development pathways, noting <cite id="7e8a3846-0">“limitations of current research”</cite> and <cite id="7e8a3846-0">“important future research avenues in order to develop effective nonchemical slug control measures.”</cite> For sciomyzids, that means replicated crop-field studies measuring establishment, dispersal, seasonal phenology, and actual reduction in slug damage and yield loss.

6. **Assess safety, selectivity, and broader ecological risk.** Any biocontrol program should include non-target and environmental risk assessment, especially because a broader review concludes that <cite id="ab0564ab-1">“biological control of nonmarine mollusc pests has generally not been demonstrated to be safe”</cite>. For *T. elata*, priorities include host specificity, effects on native gastropods, and unintended food-web consequences.

In short, the main research agenda is: <cite id="41dfe102-0">understand ecological requirements</cite>, <cite id="9699efaa-0">optimize rearing</cite>, <cite id="2cd0bdca-0">resolve prey-species effects</cite>, <cite id="2cd0bdca-0,2cd0bdca-7">test compatibility with nematode-based control</cite>, <cite id="7e8a3846-0">validate effectiveness in the field</cite>, and <cite id="ab0564ab-1">demonstrate safety and selectivity</cite>.

To accurately estimate carbon stocks in agricultural and forestry management scenarios with spatial decision support tools, you typically need a combination of **biophysical, management, and spatial-reference data**:

- **Land use / land cover data** — because carbon stocks vary strongly by land use, and fine land-use classification can improve forest carbon estimation. <cite id="9f9c31a7-1">SOC spatial variability is affected by land use.</cite> <cite id="f7c754b7-0">Fine land use classification can improve the estimation of forest carbon stocks in large areas.</cite>

- **Management practice data** — especially for agricultural soils, where models need information on how land is managed. <cite id="9f9c31a7-7">SOC models incorporate factors such as climate variables, land use, and management practices.</cite>

- **Soil data** — especially for soil organic carbon estimates, including variables such as soil depth and other soil properties. <cite id="9f9c31a7-3">SOC stock distribution was related to land use, topography, and soil depth.</cite>

- **Climate data** — temperature, rainfall, and related climatic drivers are commonly required predictors. <cite id="9f9c31a7-7">SOC models incorporate climate variables.</cite> <cite id="9f9c31a7-6">Geospatial datasets related to vegetation, climate, lithology and geology, and topography were gathered to determine predictors for SOC stocks.</cite>

- **Topography / terrain data** — elevation, slope, and terrain position often affect biomass and soil carbon distribution. <cite id="9f9c31a7-3">SOC stock distribution was related to topography.</cite> <cite id="9f9c31a7-6">Topography was among the geospatial predictors gathered for SOC stocks.</cite>

- **Vegetation / biomass / forest inventory data** — forest carbon estimation generally requires field inventory or biomass observations, often combined with remote sensing. <cite id="eb24ed21-0">Forest carbon stock dynamics were modeled using USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data.</cite> <cite id="f7c754b7-4">Remote-sensing-based carbon stock estimation is not done in isolation from in-situ or field-based inventory information; field information is crucial.</cite>

- **Remote sensing data** — satellite, LiDAR, radar, or multisensor imagery are widely used to map biomass and carbon over large areas. <cite id="e86ba2cb-1">Carbon stocks and sequestration potential can be estimated by integrating multisensory remote sensing.</cite> <cite id="f7c754b7-1">Refined forest biomass and carbon stock estimation can integrate recent advances in remote sensing.</cite>

- **Geology / lithology and related environmental covariates** — these can help explain spatial variation in soil carbon. <cite id="9f9c31a7-6">Vegetation, climate, lithology and geology, and topography were gathered as predictors for SOC stocks.</cite>

In practice, the minimum useful input set is:

1. **Spatial boundaries and land-use maps**  
2. **Soil measurements/properties**  
3. **Climate surfaces**  
4. **Topographic layers**  
5. **Vegetation/biomass or forest inventory data**  
6. **Management history and practices**  
7. **Remote sensing layers for wall-to-wall spatial coverage**

So, the short answer is: **accurate carbon-stock estimation needs spatially explicit land use, soils, climate, topography, vegetation/biomass or inventory data, management information, and usually remote-sensing inputs.** <cite id="9f9c31a7-7,9f9c31a7-6,f7c754b7-4">These factors are repeatedly identified as core predictors or requirements in SOC and forest carbon estimation.</cite>

Ganoderma triterpenoids, including ganoderic acids (GAs), are made through the **mevalonate (MVA) pathway** and then a **post-lanosterol oxidation/modification branch**.

**1) Upstream MVA stage: acetyl-CoA → mevalonate → IPP/DMAPP**  
This pathway begins from acetyl-CoA. In *Ganoderma lucidum*, genes such as <cite id="3e48682f-1">AACT, HMGS, PMK, FPS, and SQS were highly expressed across different developmental stages</cite>, showing that the canonical MVA route supplies precursors for GA production. Among these steps, **HMGS** and especially **HMGR** are important because HMGR is widely regarded as a rate-limiting control point for triterpenoid flux; a study snippet notes that <cite id="062cd490-3">three are important for the GAs biosynthesis, which are: 3-Hydroxy-3-methyglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGR)</cite>. Functionally, this stage converts acetyl-CoA into the isoprene building blocks that feed triterpene synthesis.

**2) Isoprenoid condensation stage: IPP/DMAPP → FPP → squalene**  
After mevalonate-derived C5 units are formed, they are condensed to longer prenyl intermediates. The presence and strong expression of **FPS** and **SQS** in *G. lucidum* <cite id="3e48682f-1">AACT, HMGS, PMK, FPS, and SQS were highly expressed across different developmental stages</cite> indicates their role in channeling carbon into triterpenoids. **FPS** makes farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP), and **SQS** converts FPP into squalene, committing flux toward the triterpene/sterol backbone. Consistent with this central role, a recent multiomics study found that <cite id="56c2787e-0">Zn2Cys6_61 directly binds to and activates the promoter of squalene synthase, a key enzyme in triterpenoid backbone biosynthesis</cite>.

**3) Cyclization stage: squalene/oxidosqualene → lanosterol**  
The pathway next forms the tetracyclic triterpene scaffold. One study explicitly states that <cite id="3e48682f-0">Ganoderic acid biosynthesis could be divided into two modules in G. lucidum: lanosterol and GA biosynthesis</cite>. In this framework, the first module produces **lanosterol**, the core lanostane skeleton from which GAs derive. The 2025 multiomics paper also defines GAs as <cite id="56c2787e-0">high-value lanostane-type triterpenoids derived from Ganoderma lucidum</cite>. Thus, squalene is epoxidized and cyclized to lanosterol, establishing the carbon skeleton required for ganoderic acid formation.

**4) Tailoring stage: lanosterol → ganoderic acids**  
The second module modifies lanosterol into individual GAs through oxidation and other tailoring reactions, mainly by **cytochrome P450s**. The module split is stated directly: <cite id="3e48682f-0">Ganoderic acid biosynthesis could be divided into two modules in G. lucidum: lanosterol and GA biosynthesis</cite>. For the downstream GA-specific branch, **CYP5150L8** and related P450s are especially important; transcriptomic work highlighted that <cite id="3e48682f-3">CYP5150L8</cite> is associated with GA biosynthesis, and functional characterization showed that <cite id="062cd490-4">a cytochrome P450 gene CYP512U6 from G. lucidum ... is involved in the ganoderic acid biosynthesis</cite>. These oxidative enzymes install hydroxyl, carbonyl, and carboxyl functionalities on the lanostane backbone, generating structurally diverse ganoderic acids such as ganoderic acid A, D, and others.

**Overall contribution of distinct stages and key enzymes**  
So, the MVA pathway contributes in a staged way:

- **AACT/HMGS/HMGR and related MVA enzymes** build the universal isoprenoid precursors. <cite id="3e48682f-1">AACT, HMGS, PMK, FPS, and SQS were highly expressed</cite>  
- **FPS and SQS** direct those precursors into the triterpene branch by producing FPP and then squalene. <cite id="56c2787e-0">squalene synthase, a key enzyme in triterpenoid backbone biosynthesis</cite>  
- **Lanosterol-forming steps** create the **lanostane scaffold**, since GAs are <cite id="56c2787e-0">lanostane-type triterpenoids</cite>.  
- **P450 tailoring enzymes** such as **CYP5150L8** and **CYP512U6** convert lanosterol into specific ganoderic acids. <cite id="062cd490-4">CYP512U6 ... is involved in the ganoderic acid biosynthesis</cite>

In short: the **early MVA steps determine precursor supply**, **SQS and lanosterol formation establish the triterpene backbone**, and **downstream P450 oxidations produce ganoderic acid and its analogs**.

Once microcracks start forming, the fibers transfer tensile stress across the crack faces, which <cite id="ee988992-0">improves the flexural strength and toughness of concrete</cite> and <cite id="ee988992-0">provides exceptional resistance to early and long-term cracking</cite>.

For tensile behavior, fiber addition usually helps more in <cite id="0d6e7ddf-7">post-cracking</cite> performance than in peak uncracked strength: fiber-reinforced concrete shows <cite id="0d6e7ddf-7">improved tensile strength, ductility, and most importantly, post-cracking</cite> behavior, while some studies note that <cite id="0d6e7ddf-8">polymer fibers did not influence the maximum compressive and flexural tensile strength of concrete</cite>. So the key benefit is often not a large increase in first-crack strength, but better retention of load after cracking.

For crack resistance, polymer fibers make beams develop <cite id="27d8fcf7-4">the number of cracks was increased</cite> while <cite id="27d8fcf7-4">the initial crack shear force of the beam was improved</cite>. This means cracking tends to be more distributed and finer, instead of one or two large brittle cracks. Related studies also report that polypropylene fibers <cite id="27d8fcf7-3">significantly improved the cracking behavior</cite> of reinforced concrete members.

For load-bearing capacity, the fibers raise the beam’s ability to carry load after cracking by increasing shear and flexural resistance. Evidence shows that beams with polypropylene fibers <cite id="27d8fcf7-1">improved the ultimate shear strength by 30–45%</cite>, and fiber bridging can provide <cite id="27d8fcf7-5">significant shear resistance</cite> and <cite id="27d8fcf7-5">large deformation capacity</cite>. More broadly, fiber incorporation <cite id="0d6e7ddf-1">enhances the concrete's crack resistance, tensile load capacity, and ductility in failure mode</cite>.

In short: polymer fibers help concrete beams by arresting and bridging cracks, redistributing tensile stresses, increasing toughness and ductility, reducing brittle failure, and boosting post-cracking shear/flexural load capacity.

Recommended ways to make glued-in rod timber connections ductile and avoid brittle failure are: - Provide sufficient rod embedment length and edge distance so that the rod can yield instead of the timber or bond line failing prematurely. - Use a glued-in embedment length of about 15d or more to prevent rod pull-out failure (where d is rod diameter). - For rods glued parallel to grain, explicitly verify the timber’s tension strength at the end of the steel rod, because this zone is vulnerable to brittle end splitting/tension failure. - Check and prevent brittle timber failure modes such as splitting, tensile failure of the timber member, and group tear-out, especially in multiple-rod joints. - For multiple-rod connections, ensure adequate rod spacing and edge distances to reduce splitting and group effects. - Prefer designs that promote ductile failure modes, including selecting rod/yield strength appropriately so steel yielding governs rather than brittle timber failure. - Use an adhesive with good gap-filling properties and control installation quality, since poor bonding can trigger brittle bond-line failure. In short: detail the connection so steel yielding is the governing failure mode, while providing enough embedment, spacing, edge distance, and timber-end verification to suppress pull-out, splitting, and group tear-out.

Environmental conditions matter mainly because crystalline admixtures (CAs) are <cite id="8c61c11b-0">moisture-activated systems</cite>: <cite id="8c61c11b-0">CA chemicals react with moisture and cement particles and by-products to generate C-S-H</cite>, and <cite id="8c61c11b-0">unreacted CA chemicals migrate with water through the matrix and diffuse into cracks, where they react further.</cite> As a result, <cite id="8c61c11b-0">moisture in the environment has a direct influence on the self-healing effect in mortars and concretes.</cite>

In practice:

- <cite id="8c61c11b-0">Total closure and strength regain in CA mortars was only observed under moist curing, while no healing occurred in dry air curing.</cite>
- Under long-term wet exposure, healing is much stronger: <cite id="8c61c11b-0">the ratio of healed crack area was around 70–100% after 12 months when submerged in water</cite>, compared with <cite id="8c61c11b-0">around 40% in a humidity chamber.</cite>
- <cite id="8c61c11b-0">Wet/dry cycles</cite> can still promote healing, but performance depends on how much water reaches the crack. For example, <cite id="8c61c11b-0">in mortars with 0.8% CA, the healing ratio increased from 31% after 7 days to 59% after 28 days in 95% RH and from 23% to 54% in cyclic conditions involving 2 days of immersion in water followed by 2 days at 60% RH.</cite>
- Realistic intermittent wetting can work if water contact is sufficient: <cite id="8c61c11b-0">wet/dry cycles, with at least 1 h of water contact in every cycle, can lead to nearly complete healing if the crack width does not exceed 30 μm.</cite>

Crack size also interacts strongly with the environment. <cite id="8c61c11b-0">The deposition of the healing products in the cracks strongly depended on the width of the crack and the exposure conditions.</cite> More specifically, <cite id="7d7d2a19-2">the limits were shown of the self-healing capability of crystalline admixture for cracks wider than 150 µm</cite>, so narrower cracks are much more likely to heal fully, especially under wet curing.

Temperature affects the rate of hydration/crystallization too. <cite id="8c61c11b-0">Temperature has a direct influence on the self-healing effect</cite> because <cite id="8c61c11b-0">the effect of temperature is mainly due to an acceleration in the rate of chemical and biological processes and should therefore increase the kinetics of self-healing.</cite> But <cite id="8c61c11b-0">too high temperatures can have negative consequences on the development of healing products by modifying the equilibrium of hydration products and hydration reactions.</cite>

So, in one sentence: <cite id="8c61c11b-0">water availability, exposure regime (immersion vs. wet/dry vs. dry air), crack width, and temperature</cite> largely control how well crystalline admixtures can continue hydration, form crystals/healing products, and restore watertightness and sometimes strength.

In neuroeconomics, the Ultimatum Game is treated as a realistic model of social decision-making because it captures several features that matter in everyday human interactions:

- <cite id="95ccd242-0">Social decisions are adaptive because outcomes depend on other people’s behavior, and decision makers often care about consequences to others as well as themselves.</cite> The Ultimatum Game mirrors this by forcing a person to weigh <cite id="72c8039b-8">monetary gain against the option to reject a low, but non-zero offer as a way to punish the other player</cite>.
- It reflects the fact that real people do not maximize money mechanically. In the UG, <cite id="72c8039b-2">responders often reject unfair splits even at personal cost</cite>, and <cite id="72c8039b-0">over 90% of very unfair offers below one dollar are rejected</cite>. That makes the task useful for studying how fairness norms override narrow self-interest.
- The game also resembles real social life because unfair treatment evokes emotion and norm enforcement. <cite id="72c8039b-1">Responders react to unfair offers with negative emotional feelings, which are thought to play a pivotal role in costly punishment/norm enforcement</cite>. This links decisions to both affective and regulatory brain systems rather than pure calculation.
- Neuroeconomics uses the UG precisely because it exposes the neural basis of these social motives. <cite id="72c8039b-3">The “irrational” rejection of unfair Ultimatum Game offers has been correlated with feelings</cite>, and <cite id="c9723f02-7">neuroscience studies have used the ultimatum game to understand the neuropsychological mechanisms that underlie the enforcement of fairness</cite>.
- Finally, the UG can model downstream social consequences of mistreatment. <cite id="c9723f02-5">Researchers have investigated the consequences of unfair treatment in subsequent interactions with new interaction partners and the associated neural mechanisms</cite>, which makes it relevant to how real-world social experiences shape later choices.

So, the core reason is: <cite id="c9723f02-2">the Ultimatum Game illustrates how people make decisions about fairness and cooperation</cite> under strategic interdependence, emotion, and social norms—not just financial incentives. That is why it is such a central paradigm in neuroeconomics.

ESL learners’ first-language literacy level appears to affect English spelling transfer mainly by determining <cite id="ea751d7b-4">whether they already have literacy skills that can be transferred from the first language to English</cite>. For learners who are already literate in their L1, educators are advised to <cite id="ea751d7b-4">help English learners transfer skills from first language literacy to English by pointing out similarities</cite>. In practice, this means learners with stronger L1 literacy are more likely to bring usable knowledge about print, sound structure, and symbol–sound mapping into English spelling.

By contrast, when L1 literacy is weak or underdeveloped, transfer is harder because the learner has less established metalinguistic knowledge to draw on. This fits broader evidence that <cite id="0530a897-1">alphabet knowledge and phonological awareness are strong predictors of successful literacy development</cite>; if those foundations are not well developed in the first language, learners have less basis for transferring sound-to-spelling correspondences into English.

The transfer is not just about literacy level in general, but also about the kind of literacy experience learners had. A review reports that <cite id="ea751d7b-0">the first language one was taught to read, and the instructional method by which one was taught, can have profound and long-lasting</cite> effects on later reading procedures. So, higher L1 literacy—especially literacy built through explicit attention to phonology and print—should better support transfer of phoneme–grapheme knowledge, while lower L1 literacy or non-alphabetic literacy backgrounds may leave learners needing more direct English phonics instruction.

Finally, transfer is shaped by orthographic distance. Research on English spelling in foreign/second language learners notes that <cite id="0530a897-8">three types of distance between first language (L1) and English ... may impact English spelling, namely distance in writing system</cite>. Likewise, a study on ESL orthographic knowledge found that <cite id="0530a897-5">literacy in a morphosyllabic L1 is associated with greater orthographic knowledge skills</cite>. So stronger L1 literacy generally helps, but the benefit is larger when learners’ prior literacy includes transferable awareness of how sounds and symbols relate.

In short: <cite id="ea751d7b-4,0530a897-1,ea751d7b-0">higher L1 literacy usually improves ESL learners’ ability to transfer sound-to-spelling knowledge into English, whereas low L1 literacy limits that transfer because learners have weaker alphabetic and phonological foundations to build on.</cite>

Overall, ESL learners <cite id="3d1fb6c9-0">do rely on first-language knowledge in the development of English spelling</cite>, and that influence can be <cite id="212ac2e8-1">both positive and negative</cite>. Early on, this reliance is often more visible in actual errors, since <cite id="3d1fb6c9-3">spelling errors reflected L1 interference or interlingual influences, based on structural differences between English and Spanish</cite>. But over time, as English spelling proficiency grows, learners become less dependent on L1-based strategies and more dependent on their own developing English orthographic knowledge: longitudinal work found that <cite id="6ac8c7d9-0">L1 literacy variables</cite> affect English spelling, yet <cite id="6ac8c7d9-0">English spelling measured at earlier points strongly predicted later English spelling</cite>. So the pattern is a shift from stronger early L1 transfer toward greater reliance on English-specific spelling knowledge, with L1 influence still present but less dominant.

Research on housing conditions also identifies <cite id="09ea1920-0">geographic proximity to necessary services and social opportunities</cite> as a key housing-related issue affecting workers’ health. So remote housing does not just reduce mobility; it can also increase social isolation and make it harder to reach essential services quickly, especially when workers depend on employers or informal rides.

Although program rules provide for transportation in some circumstances—<cite id="7276ac65-1">transportation modes for temporary foreign workers can be plane, train, boat, car, bus, etc.</cite>—this does not solve everyday local access problems once workers are living in remote farm housing. Overall, remote housing tends to make workers more dependent on employers for travel and more vulnerable to delayed or limited access to essential services.

When the outcome is <cite id="b33cb101-2">prevention of bacterial infection and colonization</cite>, the available evidence favors N95 respirators over surgical masks: a CDC evidence review reported that <cite id="b33cb101-2">N95 respirators were more effective than surgical masks for the prevention of bacterial infection and colonization</cite>, with a <cite id="b33cb101-2">pooled RR: 0.46 (95%CI: 0.34–0.62)</cite>. Supporting summaries also note that <cite id="b33cb101-3">surgical mask users exhibited a lower protection efficacy compared to N95 users for bacterial infection</cite>.

On user comfort, the tradeoff generally goes the other way: N95s tend to be less comfortable and more burdensome to wear for long periods. A consensus report notes <cite id="d32a2f66-5">drawbacks in terms of comfort and fit</cite> for <cite id="d32a2f66-5">disposable N95 respirators</cite>, and prolonged-wear studies were designed specifically to measure <cite id="d32a2f66-0">discomfort and level of exertion experienced by health care workers while wearing respiratory</cite> protection. Reviews also report that <cite id="d32a2f66-3">the side effects of surgical and N95 masks include skin, respiratory, cardiac, and neurological</cite>, with discomfort commonly emphasized for N95 use.

So, in short: <cite id="b33cb101-2,b33cb101-3">N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks at reducing airborne bacterial pathogens</cite>, but <cite id="d32a2f66-5,d32a2f66-0">they usually impose a greater comfort/tolerance burden on users</cite>. Surgical masks are generally more comfortable, but they provide less protection against airborne bacterial exposure.

Randomized controlled trials assess this by <cite id="dba99795-1,cec3a88d-9,cec3a88d-1">directly comparing time from enrollment to hospital discharge between convalescent-plasma and control groups</cite>. In major hospitalized-patient RCTs, the discharge times were very similar or slightly worse with plasma: <cite id="dba99795-1">13 vs 12 days</cite> in one NEJM trial, <cite id="cec3a88d-9">12 vs 11 days</cite> in the RECOVERY trial, and <cite id="cec3a88d-1">6 vs 4 days</cite> in a placebo-controlled trial; a review of trials also noted <cite id="cec3a88d-5">the REMAP-CAP trial reported 44 vs 39 days</cite>. Meta-analyses then pool these randomized comparisons and generally conclude there is <cite id="cec3a88d-0">no difference in time to hospital discharge</cite> and that convalescent plasma <cite id="cec3a88d-4,cec3a88d-6">does not significantly improve clinical improvement or time to clinical improvement</cite>. So, overall, both RCTs and meta-analyses indicate that convalescent plasma <cite id="cec3a88d-0,cec3a88d-4,cec3a88d-6">does not meaningfully shorten hospital discharge time for hospitalized COVID-19 patients</cite>.

Overall, PVP-I looks <cite id="4f3a8396-0">consistently potent in vitro</cite> but only <cite id="4f3a8396-0">modestly and variably effective in clinical use, with results differing by setting, site treated, administration method, and specimen type</cite>.

**In vitro inactivation**
- <cite id="b86bc10c-5">Povidone-iodine nasal antiseptic solutions at concentrations as low as 0.5% rapidly inactivate SARS-CoV-2 at contact times as short as 15 seconds.</cite>
- Multiple lab studies cited in clinical literature report that <cite id="b86bc10c-0">SARS-CoV-2 was completely inactivated in vitro at variable PVP-I concentrations of 0.5%, 1.25%, and 2.5%</cite>.
- For nasal formulations specifically, <cite id="73f99406-1">0.5% PVP-I nasal spray is rapidly virucidal to SARS-CoV-2 in vitro</cite> and <cite id="b86bc10c-1">this effect occurs with as little as 15 seconds of contact</cite>.
- Oral-rinse literature also indicates strong activity: <cite id="b86bc10c-2">PVP-I was effective in killing SARS-CoV-2 and showed higher virucidal activity than other commonly used active ingredients</cite>.

**Clinical reduction of viral load**
- In a double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of <cite id="1c054a58-0">0.5% PVP-I nasal drops plus 20 mL gargle for at least 30 seconds in 32 mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients</cite>, <cite id="1c054a58-0">the mean change in viral titers versus control was not statistically significant (P = 0.109)</cite>, but <cite id="1c054a58-0">the mean change in Ct value was borderline statistically significant (P = 0.042)</cite>. The authors concluded that <cite id="1c054a58-0">0.5% PVP-I has an effect on reducing nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal viral loads</cite>.
- Another clinical line of evidence suggests repeated nasal dosing may work better: <cite id="7e256e90-2">20 doses of 0.5% Nasodine® nasal spray over 2.5 days significantly reduced viable SARS-CoV-2 titers in the nasal cavity</cite>.
- For oral formulations, a randomized trial found that after a <cite id="1bd9519a-0">30-second rinse with 2% povidone-iodine mouthwash</cite>, <cite id="1bd9519a-0">Ct values increased significantly in the PI group at 30 minutes (P < 0.05)</cite>, whereas <cite id="1bd9519a-0">chlorhexidine and the herbal mouthwash did not show significant differences</cite>. The study concluded that <cite id="1bd9519a-0">PI mouthwash might potentially reduce spread of SARS-CoV-2, especially in dental settings</cite>.
- The broader review perspective is cautious: <cite id="4f3a8396-0">despite supportive in vitro data, clinical findings differ depending on whether treatment is nasal, oral, or pharyngeal; whether given as rinse, gargle, or spray; and whether outcomes are measured in nasopharyngeal or saliva samples</cite>.

**Practical interpretation by concentration/formulation**
- **0.5% nasal antiseptic/spray:** strongest evidence for rapid lab inactivation <cite id="b86bc10c-5">within 15 seconds</cite>; clinical benefit appears plausible but mixed, with <cite id="1c054a58-0">borderline/limited short-term RCT effects</cite> and <cite id="7e256e90-2">better results in a repeated-dose Phase II study</cite>.
- **0.5% nasal drops + gargle:** may lower upper-airway viral burden, but the effect size in short-term RCT testing was <cite id="1c054a58-0">not clearly significant for viral titers</cite>.
- **2% mouthwash:** appears clinically promising for saliva, with <cite id="1bd9519a-0">significant Ct increase after a 30-second rinse and 30-minute follow-up</cite>.
- **1.25% and 2.5% formulations:** supportive evidence is mainly preclinical; <cite id="b86bc10c-0">they have been reported to completely inactivate SARS-CoV-2 in vitro</cite>, but the snippets here do not provide comparable clinical trial data.

**Bottom line**
<cite id="b86bc10c-5">PVP-I is highly effective at inactivating SARS-CoV-2 in vitro, even at 0.5% with very short contact times.</cite> In patients, <cite id="1c054a58-0">short-term reductions in naso/oropharyngeal viral burden are suggestive but not uniformly statistically robust</cite>, while <cite id="1bd9519a-0">2% mouthwash shows a clearer short-term salivary effect</cite>. So the best-supported conclusion is that PVP-I is a strong topical virucide, but <cite id="4f3a8396-0">its real-world clinical effectiveness depends on concentration, formulation, dosing frequency, and sampling method, and remains less consistent than the lab data</cite>.

In non-ICU COVID-19 patients, these correlations can be used as a practical **early-risk stratification tool**:

1. **Hyponatremia should raise concern for worse lung involvement.**  
   In one non-ICU-focused observational cohort, <cite id="76ff1766-0">hyponatremia was common and was associated with indices of pulmonary dysfunction</cite>. More broadly, another retrospective COVID-19 study found that <cite id="106280f7-0">hyponatremia was present in 44% of patients</cite> and that <cite id="a0cb156b-0">hyponatremia patients required significantly higher rates of ICU admissions and oxygen support</cite>.  
   **Clinical implication:** if a ward patient presents with low sodium, treat that as a warning sign to monitor respiratory status more closely and reassess oxygen needs sooner.

2. **Low sodium plus poor oxygenation suggests higher short-term deterioration risk.**  
   The sodium/pulmonary dysfunction study reported that <cite id="a0cb156b-1">hyponatremia, mostly of mild grade, was common among the studied COVID-19 patients and was associated with indices of pulmonary dysfunctions</cite>.  
   **Clinical implication:** a non-ICU patient with both hyponatremia and worsening oxygenation index should be considered for:
   - more frequent vitals/SpO₂ checks,
   - earlier arterial blood gas or imaging reassessment,
   - earlier escalation of oxygen therapy,
   - lower threshold for step-up care/ICU review if respiratory metrics worsen.

3. **High IL-6 can help identify inflammatory-driven hyponatremia.**  
   Evidence from the COVIVA-related report shows that <cite id="a0cb156b-4">IL-6 levels were inversely correlated with plasma sodium levels</cite>. Also, the retrospective analysis suggested that <cite id="a0cb156b-0">monitoring inflammatory markers</cite> may be useful in hyponatremic COVID-19 patients.  
   **Clinical implication:** when hyponatremia coexists with elevated IL-6, clinicians should suspect that the low sodium may reflect a stronger inflammatory state rather than simple dehydration alone. That can support:
   - closer review for cytokine-driven deterioration,
   - more careful fluid decisions,
   - consideration of anti-inflammatory treatment when otherwise indicated by guidelines and overall severity.

4. **These markers can guide fluids and escalation decisions, but sodium should not be corrected reflexively.**  
   Because hyponatremia in COVID-19 may track inflammation and pulmonary severity, it should prompt an assessment of cause rather than automatic saline administration.  
   **Clinical implication:** evaluate volume status, medications, renal function, and possible SIADH; avoid overhydration in patients with respiratory compromise; and use the combined pattern of **hyponatremia + worsening oxygenation + high IL-6** to justify earlier senior review and tighter monitoring.

**Bottom line:**  
<cite id="a0cb156b-1">Hyponatremia is associated with pulmonary dysfunction</cite>, and <cite id="a0cb156b-4">higher IL-6 is linked to lower sodium</cite>. So in non-ICU COVID-19 patients, the combination of **low sodium, impaired oxygenation, and elevated IL-6** should be treated as a marker of potentially more severe inflammatory lung disease—supporting **closer monitoring, cautious fluid management, earlier oxygen escalation, and a lower threshold for step-up care**.

In risk-of-bias frameworks for randomized trials, <cite id="dddbcc00-6">performance bias is linked to the masking/blinding of participants and personnel</cite>, and <cite id="54b12d06-0">blinding of outcome assessors can still be possible even when blinding participants and personnel is not feasible</cite>. For Tai Chi trials on depressive symptoms, this matters a great deal because <cite id="81adc639-2">it is often impossible to blind Tai Chi coaches and participants</cite>; accordingly, one recent review reported that <cite id="81adc639-1">the risk of performance bias was high in four trials because participants were not blinded in the active intervention</cite>, while <cite id="7150c825-1">four trials were rated low risk for performance bias when blinding of participants and personnel was described</cite>. This is especially important for depression outcomes because <cite id="54b12d06-2">subjective, self-reported outcomes in unblinded studies are at risk of bias</cite>. So, in Tai Chi depression RCTs, lack of participant/personnel blinding tends to push performance-bias judgments toward high risk, whereas successful blinding lowers that rating; assessor-only blinding helps detection bias more than performance bias <cite id="54b12d06-0,81adc639-2">even if evaluator or statistician blinding is used</cite>.

The best direct evidence I found is a 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials. It specifically separated studies into <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">“(1) a combination of Tai Chi and antidepressants versus standard antidepressants”</cite> and reported that <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">“The Tai Chi intervention showed improvements in mental and physical well-being as evidenced by the reductions in depression and anxiety and improved quality of life (QOL)”</cite>.

So, the overall evidence suggests that <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">adding Tai Chi to antidepressants is more effective than antidepressants alone for reducing depressive symptoms</cite>. However, the same review also notes that <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">“Further well-controlled RCTs are recommended with a precision trial design and larger sample sizes”</cite>, which means the result is promising but not yet definitive.

In short: <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">Tai Chi as an adjunct to antidepressants appears to improve depressive symptoms more than antidepressants alone</cite>, but <cite id="f1ce5cc8-0">the evidence base is still limited and would benefit from larger, better-controlled trials</cite>.

Evidence from recent China data suggests that private health insurance (PHI), when added on top of social health insurance, is associated with <cite id="7f519dad-0">changes in both outpatient and inpatient use, but the direction and size differ by population group.</cite>

- In a national study using the 2018 China National Health Services Survey, researchers compared PHI purchasers and non-purchasers within China’s three main social insurance groups: <cite id="7f519dad-0">urban employee-based basic medical insurance (UEBMI), urban resident-based basic medical insurance (URBMI), and the new rural cooperative medical scheme (NRCMS).</cite>
- The study’s regression results found that <cite id="7f519dad-0">UEBMI participants with PHI had a higher probability of both outpatient visits and inpatient admissions.</cite>
- For rural enrollees, the pattern was different: <cite id="7f519dad-0">NRCMS participants with PHI had a lower probability of outpatient visits but a higher probability of inpatient admissions.</cite>
- The paper’s summary also states that, overall, <cite id="f27aa0a3-1,9cec80a3-5">possession of PHI was associated with increased utilization of outpatient and inpatient healthcare services among participants covered by social health insurance.</cite>

A key nuance is that raw use rates and adjusted results are not identical. In simple descriptive comparisons, <cite id="7f519dad-0">participants with PHI actually showed lower observed outpatient visit rates and lower inpatient admission rates than those without PHI across UEBMI, URBMI, and NRCMS</cite>—for example, <cite id="7f519dad-0">among UEBMI participants with PHI, the outpatient visit rate was 17.9% and the inpatient admission rate was 12.4%, versus 23.6% and 15.2% among those without PHI.</cite> This means the positive association found in regression models likely reflects differences after adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, not just unadjusted averages.

Across populations, the main takeaway is:

1. <cite id="7f519dad-0">Urban employee populations (UEBMI) appear to increase both outpatient and inpatient use when enrolled in PHI.</cite>  
2. <cite id="7f519dad-0">Rural populations under NRCMS show a more selective response: less outpatient use but more inpatient use with PHI.</cite>  
3. <cite id="7f519dad-0">Effects were analyzed separately across UEBMI, URBMI, and NRCMS, indicating that PHI’s influence is heterogeneous rather than uniform across China’s insured populations.</cite>

So, the short answer is: <cite id="7f519dad-0,f27aa0a3-1">private health insurance enrollment in China tends to be associated with greater healthcare utilization after adjustment, but its effect differs by population—raising both outpatient and inpatient use among urban employee enrollees, while among rural enrollees it is linked to more inpatient but less outpatient use.</cite>

Since 2013, WHO’s pediatric ART initiation guidance has broadened from age-limited universal treatment to full “treat all.”

- In 2013, WHO recommended ART <cite id="f84fb97a-2">irrespective of CD4 count for all children with HIV under 5 years</cite>.
- Subsequent WHO guidance expanded eligibility stepwise; one summary of WHO guideline evolution notes that recommendations were broadened to <cite id="4b2d7923-1">include children aged <2, <5, and <15 years, respectively, regardless of clinical or immunologic status</cite>.
- By the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, the policy became universal: <cite id="4b2d7923-2">immediate initiation of antiretroviral therapy for everyone living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count</cite>, and WHO <cite id="4b2d7923-8">removes all limitations on eligibility for ART among people living with HIV; all populations and age groups are now eligible for treatment</cite>.

These guideline changes were intended to support global HIV treatment targets, especially the UNAIDS targets:
- <cite id="275e9bd7-1">the ambitious 90-90-90 target demands dramatic progress in closing the treatment gap for children</cite>;
- for children specifically, <cite id="275e9bd7-3">the “90-90-90” targets aim to have 90% of all children living with HIV diagnosed, 90% of those diagnosed receiving treatment, and 90% of those on treatment virally suppressed</cite>;
- and this agenda has since been extended <cite id="275e9bd7-7">to meet 95-95-95 targets by 2030</cite>.

So, in brief: WHO moved from recommending ART for all HIV-positive children under 5 in 2013 to recommending ART for all children/adolescents and ultimately all people with HIV regardless of age or CD4 count by 2016, in support of the global 90-90-90 and later 95-95-95 HIV targets.

Across Sub-Saharan Africa, HIV prevalence among TB patients has shown a strong regional gradient: <cite id="S6">in 2019, the estimated prevalence among TB cases was about 43% in southern Africa, 28% in eastern Africa, 16% in central Africa, and 8% in western Africa</cite>. At the country level, this means <cite id="S1">high TB/HIV burden countries in Sub-Saharan Africa were generally around 30% overall, with some countries in southern Africa exceeding 50%</cite>.

Examples from individual settings show the same pattern of especially high prevalence in southern Africa. In Zimbabwe, <cite id="S2">HIV prevalence among TB patients rose from 9.5% in 1985 to 74.2% in 1995, then declined slightly but remained very high at 69.6% in 2003 and 68.4% in 2008</cite>. In a South African subdistrict, <cite id="S4">HIV prevalence among newly notified TB patients was estimated at 80% in 2013</cite>. Other settings have also reported declines over time: <cite id="S8">one study found prevalence among TB patients fell from a peak of 53.6% in 2009 to 39.6% in 2013</cite>, and in Ethiopia <cite id="S7">TB/HIV coinfection declined over ten years from 45.3% to 24.5%</cite>.

Within countries, there can also be marked subregional variation. For example, in Nigeria, <cite id="S3">TB/HIV coinfection ranged from 12.3% in the North West to 44.4% in the South East</cite>, and a later estimate similarly found <cite id="S5">13.3% in the North-West versus 40.9% in the South-East</cite>. In Ethiopia, <cite id="S7">regional prevalence ranged from 16.1% in Afar to 41.9% in Addis Ababa</cite>.

Overall, the broad time trend appears to be: rapid increases during the expansion of the HIV epidemic, especially in southern Africa; then stabilization or decline in many places in the ART era, though <cite id="S1,S6">prevalence among TB patients remains highest in southern and eastern Sub-Saharan Africa and much lower in western and central Africa</cite>.

In the exhibition literature on socio-scientific issues (SSIs), critical reflection is treated as one of the core features of an SSI exhibition: <cite id="dd2ccca7-0">Yun et al. [2022], suggest three characteristics of SSI exhibitions: critical reflection, contextualized information, ...</cite> and <cite id="dd2ccca7-2">... (critical reflection, contextualized information, and opinion sharing), to provide curators a direction for a socio-scientific issues based exhibition planning.</cite>

So, in this context, critical reflection is not just “thinking about science,” but encouraging visitors to examine <cite id="628f6d3e-0">interests, concerns, values and ideas about motives and purposes of R&I</cite> around contested science-and-society topics. It is used in exhibitions because SSI-oriented informal science settings are increasingly <cite id="8c96a36b-0">engaging with critical issues at the intersection of science, technology, and society, and are looking to promote active participation from the public</cite> and to <cite id="8c96a36b-0">challenge dominant narratives and ways of (re)presenting science</cite>.

Implementation in exhibitions generally happens through three linked design moves:

1. **Presenting contextualized information**  
   Exhibitions situate the science in real social controversies rather than presenting decontextualized facts. This is part of the SSI model itself: <cite id="dd2ccca7-0">three characteristics of SSI exhibitions: critical reflection, contextualized information, ...</cite>

2. **Creating opportunities for opinion sharing and dialogue**  
   SSI exhibitions are designed to stimulate discussion, not only individual learning. The literature describes them as having the capacity to <cite id="8e92bf96-4">stimulate learning through reflection and discourse</cite>. Likewise, inclusive reflection requires settings where people <cite id="628f6d3e-0">meet to reflect on, and exchange, interests, concerns, values and ideas</cite>.

3. **Using participatory/interactive formats that support public engagement**  
   In science museums, reflection is implemented through exhibit designs that involve visitors as participants rather than passive viewers. The field describes a turn toward <cite id="8c96a36b-0">promot[ing] active participation from the public</cite>, and related museum work highlights <cite id="e7d4e224-7">Participatory exhibits are both social and visitor-determined</cite>. Prototype work on controversial research topics similarly frames museums as spaces for <cite id="628f6d3e-0">facilitating reflection on R&I framing</cite>.

Concise answer: SSI exhibitions define critical reflection as visitors’ examination of the social, ethical, and value-laden dimensions of science, and they implement it by combining <cite id="dd2ccca7-0">critical reflection, contextualized information,</cite> and <cite id="dd2ccca7-2">opinion sharing</cite> in participatory exhibit environments that foster <cite id="8e92bf96-4">reflection and discourse</cite>.

In surgical technique, <cite id="464d5660-0">a midline (median) episiotomy starts close to the midline of the perineum and extends downward in a straight line</cite>, whereas <cite id="464d5660-0">a mediolateral episiotomy begins similarly but extends laterally at a 60-degree angle</cite>. A practical consequence of technique is that <cite id="2198599a-2">because of muscle involvement, a mediolateral episiotomy may give rise to more bleeding than a midline episiotomy</cite>. Also, <cite id="2198599a-6">a midline incision is done vertically, while a mediolateral incision is done at an angle</cite>, and <cite id="2198599a-6">the mediolateral cut is less likely to tear into the anal area</cite>.

For postpartum dyspareunia, the available evidence does not show a clear advantage of one type over the other. <cite id="14a67b23-0">The only prospective observational study cited in the search results found no difference in dyspareunia or perineal pain after midline episiotomy, mediolateral episiotomy, and lateral episiotomy at 3 months postpartum</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="14a67b23-2">there is no concrete evidence that episiotomy is associated with dyspareunia</cite>, and <cite id="2198599a-1">although midline episiotomy has been suggested to offer better future sexual function</cite>, that appears to be a proposed advantage rather than a firmly established outcome.

So, in brief: <cite id="464d5660-0,2198599a-6">midline = straight vertical incision in the midline; mediolateral = angled incision away from the midline</cite>. <cite id="2198599a-6,2198599a-2">Mediolateral may better protect against extension into the anal sphincter but can involve more tissue and bleeding</cite>. <cite id="14a67b23-0,14a67b23-2">Regarding postpartum dyspareunia, current evidence suggests little or no meaningful difference between midline and mediolateral episiotomy.</cite>

Masters and Johnson’s model explains sexual functioning comprehensively by describing <cite id="b9ec5121-1">a sequence of four stages: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution</cite> and by showing that <cite id="8c6fcda8-1">the basic pattern of these stages is similar in both sexes</cite>. In the first phase, <cite id="b9ec5121-0">heart rate and breathing begin to quicken during excitement</cite>; during plateau, <cite id="b9ec5121-5">sexual excitement intensifies with increased circulation and heart rate in both sexes</cite>. The model then includes orgasm and the return to baseline in resolution, while also accounting for male–female differences in recovery: <cite id="b9ec5121-3">men typically have a greater refractory period and cannot achieve an immediately successive orgasm</cite>, whereas <cite id="8dfb5896-0">some females can return to orgasm with further stimulation and may experience additional orgasms</cite>. Together, this makes the model a broad explanation of sexual functioning because it covers <cite id="8c6fcda8-5">the physical and emotional responses individuals experience during sexual activity</cite> across both males and females.

Tidal flow constructed wetlands enhance pollutant removal mainly because <cite id="136e6da6-0">the oxygen transfer rate is much higher in tidal flow wetlands than in conventional constructed wetlands</cite>. In tidal systems, the bed is <cite id="1adeb5d2-3">continually fill[ed] and drain[ed]</cite>, which repeatedly draws air into the pore spaces during drainage and expels it during reflooding. This engineered aeration creates much more aerobic contact than in conventional subsurface wetlands, where oxygen supply is often the main limitation.

That higher oxygen availability improves removal of oxygen-demanding pollutants and ammonia: <cite id="1adeb5d2-6">tidal flow operation has shown the potential to enhance the removal of BOD5 through aerobic decomposition and the removal of ammoniacal-nitrogen</cite>. In other words, tidal flow better supports nitrifying bacteria, so ammonium is more effectively oxidized to nitrate.

For nitrogen specifically, tidal flow wetlands strengthen the full biological nitrogen pathway because <cite id="1adeb5d2-3">Nitrogen removal is a two-step process, nitrification followed by denitrification</cite>. The alternating flooded and drained phases help provide these different redox conditions in sequence: aerobic periods promote nitrification, while anoxic zones/times allow denitrification. More generally, <cite id="1adeb5d2-7">microsites with steep oxygen gradients can be established, which allow nitrification and denitrification</cite>. As a result, tidal flow wetlands can achieve <cite id="136e6da6-3">vastly improved aeration and hence outstanding total nitrogen removal compared to traditional wetland systems</cite>.

So, compared with conventional constructed wetlands, tidal flow systems work better because they:
1. <cite id="136e6da6-0">increase oxygen transfer</cite>,
2. <cite id="1adeb5d2-6">boost aerobic degradation of organics and ammonium oxidation</cite>, and
3. <cite id="1adeb5d2-3,1adeb5d2-7">better couple nitrification and denitrification through alternating aerobic/anoxic conditions and oxygen gradients</cite>.

Placement tests help EFL teachers <cite id="e242e671-7,e242e671-2">identify a learner’s reading level and place the learner into an appropriate graded-reader level</cite>, which makes it easier to select texts that are neither too easy nor too difficult. This matters because <cite id="cd186c14-0">comprehensible input must be understandable to learners</cite>, and readers should <cite id="cd186c14-3">begin with texts with a very limited vocabulary range and then move to texts with gradually increasing vocabulary ranges</cite>. When placement is accurate, students are more likely to receive “i+1”-type input—slightly above their current level—which research suggests supports development: <cite id="02555e38-1">EFL learners exposed to i+1 input improved reading comprehension</cite>. So, placement tests support reading growth by matching learners with appropriately leveled materials that provide comprehensible, progressively challenging input.

In grammatical error correction (GEC), back-translation has been <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">adapted by reversing the usual GEC training direction: a sequence-to-sequence model is trained to transform grammatical text into ungrammatical text, then applied to grammatical monolingual corpora to create synthetic erroneous source sentences paired with the original clean sentences as pseudo-parallel GEC data.</cite> The survey notes that <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">this is also called “reverse-noising,” and unlike MT back-translation, it does not involve a third language.</cite>

In terms of evaluation, this adaptation has mainly been assessed through downstream GEC performance on standard benchmarks. The survey reports that <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">Kasewa et al. (2018) found gains of 1.98 M² on CoNLL-2014 and 6.08 GLEU on JFLEG</cite>, while <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">Lichtarge et al. (2019) reported a 14.9-point F0.5 increase over a comparable baseline on the restricted W&I+LOCNESS track of the BEA-2019 shared task.</cite> These results suggest that <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">back-translated synthetic data greatly improves GEC performance, especially in low-resource settings.</cite>

Researchers have also evaluated back-translation beyond raw benchmark scores by examining the quality of the synthetic data itself. The literature summarized in the survey indicates that <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">directly generated-and-filtered errors tend to look more realistic than rule-based artificial errors, but synthetic errors are still not identical to naturally occurring learner errors.</cite> For example, <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">Choe et al. (2019) found that 39% of edits in their synthetic data did not appear in NUCLE, Lang-8, or FCE training data</cite>, which has been taken as evidence that realism remains an issue.

Another line of evaluation concerns scale and filtering. Early work often assumed that <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">very large amounts of pseudo-data—such as 1.26 million sentences in Kasewa et al. (2018) and 100 million in Lichtarge et al. (2019)—would help without explicit quality filtering.</cite> More recent findings complicate that assumption: <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">Yasunaga et al. (2021) showed that small amounts of synthetic data from a weaker system can outperform data from a stronger system, and Yuan and Bryant (2021) showed stronger generators help only when outputs are carefully filtered.</cite>

Finally, the benchmark setup used to evaluate these methods is fairly standardized: <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">CoNLL-2014 is typically evaluated with M²/F0.5-style scoring, JFLEG with GLEU, and BEA-2019 with W&I+LOCNESS and ERRANT F0.5.</cite>

So, in short: <cite id="43d9fcbf-0">back-translation in GEC has been adapted as monolingual error generation via reversed GEC models, and evaluated both by downstream gains on CoNLL-2014, JFLEG, and BEA-2019 and by analyses of synthetic-data realism, quantity, and filtering.</cite>
